Superior General of the Daughters of Saint Anne

To her dearest Daughters

Presentation

The little volume I present to you does not bear, as you might expect, the title “ACTS OF THE CHAPTER,” but rather “BASIC DOCUMENTS,” because in reality it constitutes only one part of the “ACTS” of the Special Chapter celebrated by our Congregation in two sessions: September 1 - November 30, 1969, and September 1, 1970 - January 26, 1971.

The second part of the “Acts” will consist of the text of the new Constitutions and the Directories that the Commission specially appointed by the Chapter Assembly is preparing and which, with God's help, will soon see the light.

* * *

In past years, through my circular Letters and the exhortations I had occasion to address to you during Visitations, during the many retreats, and at Meetings, I certainly did not fail to draw your attention to the decisive importance of the period our Institute had begun to live:

“If every General Chapter,” I wrote in my Letter convoking the Special General Chapter on December 29, 1968, “must be a milestone on the path of a religious Congregation, the one we are preparing to celebrate must not be a mere milestone but a decisive and irreversible stage, from which our Religious Family will resume its journey not only more deeply aware of the sublime dignity of its specific vocation and the seriousness of its commitments, but also enlightened and strengthened by a new ‘code of life’ which, being the fruit of the prayer, meditation and passionate study of all, will bear the authentic stamp of our spirituality.”

I can affirm that throughout the Chapter this “passionate study” never flagged on the part of the Capitulars, just as the support of your prayer and sacrifice never failed on the part of all of you. Indeed, there were generous souls who, afflicted by most painful and mortal illnesses, gladly offered their sufferings and their very lives to the Lord to obtain a true and radical renewal of our Congregation. From Heaven they surely continue to implore divine help for the full and complete accomplishment of the work whose beginning on earth they assisted in the most fruitful and meritorious way.

The Chapter Assembly, guided by the directives of the Council Documents and the Motu Proprio “Ecclesiae Sanctae,” devoted itself from the very first days to studying the two essential aspects of the renewal of religious life:

  • the “return to the sources of every form of Christian life and to the original spirit” of the Institute;

  • the adaptation of the Institute “to the changed conditions of the times” (Cf. P.C. 2).

    • It immediately realized, however, the need first of all to study in depth, according to the new conciliar themes, the general principles of religious life, both in themselves and in relation to the new social situations and the related pastoral needs of the countries where the Institute carries out its activity. This in-depth study took up the whole of the first session.

    During the interval between the first and second sessions, the intersessional Commission directed its work toward researching and examining the documents concerning the origins of our Institute; in this way the material was prepared that the Chapter Assembly needed in order to know and interpret the charism of the Mother Foundress and hence the characteristic spirituality of our Congregation.

    This second phase of study revealed to us the existence, largely unsuspected, of a spiritual heritage of incalculable value, which made us realize, almost for the first time, that our spirituality, through the providential presence of Saint Anne, draws its unmistakable distinctiveness directly from the sources of Sacred Scripture, just as, in full harmony with the orientations of Vatican II, it expresses its perennial relevance.

    When the Chapter Assembly judged that it had sufficiently gathered the elements needed to define our genuine spirituality, it charged a special Commission with drawing up the list of topics into which the text of the new Constitutions was to be divided, as into so many chapters.

    This Commission submitted to the Assembly an outline which, after thorough discussion, was unanimously approved. Here it is:

    Our Religious Family in the Church

  • Purpose and spirituality of the institute

  • The consecrated community...

  • in virginity of heart (chastity)

  • for the possession of the supreme Good (poverty)

  • in the sacrament of the Father's will (obedience)

  • ...Lives in charity

  • in communion of prayer

  • in communion of life

  • ... At the service of our brothers and sisters.

  • Formation: a lifelong commitment.

  • Structures of government.

    • Once the outline was approved, the Assembly divided into Commissions and subcommissions, each charged with drafting a Basic Document corresponding to one part of the outline; each Document was to be developed so as to achieve and highlight the synthesis between the general principles of religious life worked out in the first session and the specific elements of our spirituality drawn from the Documents of our Institute's origins.

    The fact that each Document was drafted by a different group made differences of style and approach inevitable; the content, however, was submitted to careful examination, general discussion and finally approval by the Assembly through secret ballot. And you will notice, I hope, that all of them strive to express with equal fidelity the charism of the Institute, each developing one aspect of it, according to the teaching on religious life worked out by Vatican II.

    The general title of the work, “Our Religious Family in the Church,” already clearly indicates the new, more clearly and consciously ecclesial perspective on consecrated life.

    The first Document, “Purpose and Spirituality of the Institute,” sets out the rich charismatic and theological content of our Rule of 1869: “The purpose of our vocation as Daughters of Saint Anne is to guide us toward holiness, identifying ourselves with Christ in the mystery of his poverty, in imitation of Mary, daughter of Saint Anne, so as to continue in the Church, under the guidance of the holy Mother, her motherly mission.” This specific purpose of ours is completed, enriched and made fully relevant by notes drawn from the Council Documents in general, and particularly from “Lumen Gentium” and “Perfectae Caritatis.”

    The second Document, “The Consecrated Community,” highlights the more intimate bond by which the baptized person is united with Christ, following him unconditionally in order to cooperate in the saving mission of the Son of God, in a vital commitment to adhere to the Father's will under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

    It also extols the liberating power of the evangelical counsels, by virtue of which the Daughter of Saint Anne, freed from every earthly tie and rich with the poverty of Christ, fulfills her essential purpose, which is to be, already in this life, a “sign” of spiritual realities and eternal Goods, as well as an instrument of progress and uplift for her brothers and sisters.

    The third Document, “The Consecrated Community Lives in Charity: in communion of prayer - in communion of life,” clarifies and develops the concept of community life.

    Already the Rule of 1869, by repeatedly affirming that each Community of the Daughters of Saint Anne must be “a copy and a continuation of the Family of the holy Mother,” highlighted its two fundamental elements:

  • its charismatic nature;

  • the genuine family spirit that unites the Community around the Eucharistic table, in prayer, in the sharing of spiritual and material goods, in joys and sorrows, in apostolic collaboration.

    • It then draws new reasons for commending unity and fraternal charity from no. 15 of Perfectae Caritatis, which assures that the Community living “as a family united in the name of the Lord” enjoys the joy of his presence and acquires great “energy for the apostolate.”

    The fourth Document, “The Consecrated Community at the Service of Our Brothers and Sisters,” after clarifying the markedly ecclesial nature of the apostolic vocation of the Daughters of Saint Anne and the inseparable unity of contemplation and apostolic action, develops this second aspect of our spirituality and points to new ways and new methods for the pastoral renewal of the Institute in relation to the present social context.

    The fifth Document, “Formation, a Lifelong Commitment,” sets out the fundamental requirements of formation for religious life and the problems connected with it in this particular historical and social context. Starting from the idea of religious vocation in general and going on to explore the particular aspect of the vocation to the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne, it then indicates the general norms and practical criteria to be followed in the various stages of formation.

    The sixth Document sets out the “Outline of the Structure of Government of the Institute.”

    * * *

    Let me tell you that in handing you this first fruit of the work of our Special Chapter I feel immense joy. I feel that the Lord has truly granted a desire of mine which, from the first moment he allowed the tremendous responsibility of guiding our Family to be laid upon me, was my greatest concern and the object of my unceasing prayers: the desire, that is, to know clearly, soundly and surely the essence of our characteristic spirituality, so that I might guide you without uncertainty or deviation along the path the Holy Spirit originally indicated to Mother Rosa.

    The serious and committed research carried out during the Chapter and its present fruits are for me a consoling source of light and serenity. So, I hope with all my soul, they will be for you a light and an incentive to take up with fresh energy and sure direction the fundamental commitment of your sanctification and your apostolic activity.

    The Documents will soon be followed by the “norms” which, together with the spiritual principles, will form the new Constitutions and the various Directories. But observance of the norms, which the Chapter in any case wished to be simple and sober, would be worth nothing if you did not know how to infuse them with the spirituality expressed in the Documents. Just as a body is only a corpse when it is not informed and enlivened by the soul, so “regular observance” that is limited to material respect for the norms or the precept and is not inspired by a personal demand for fidelity and consistency is something dead and sterile.

    In this regard, allow me to remind you of what I wrote in the Circular already quoted:

    “There will certainly follow, as the Motu Proprio ‘Ecclesiae Sanctae’ (art. 6) wisely provides, the subsequent cautious and careful experimentation with what the Chapter has decided; but the experimentation will concern details, particular norms, the arrangement of methods and works, certainly not the spirit; the spirit must be alive and active from this moment: a spirit grounded in faith, hope and charity, in deep respect for the fundamental value of Baptism sublimated by religious consecration; a spirit sustained by the sense of responsibility that rests on each of us from the time when, having been the object of a choice on God's part, we freely accepted it and committed ourselves to love him with all our being and to serve him in the person of his favorites: the poor, the suffering, the young and children.”

    And I went on to urge you to pray that the Lord might dispose your spirit to listen “humbly, attentively, docilely” to the manifestation of his will regarding our life and the life of our Institute.

    Now the light has come; the Lord has made us understand his will; it is up to you to welcome it humbly, adhere to it docilely and carry it out faithfully, in your life and in your works.

    The new face of the Congregation will derive not so much from what the Special Chapter has decided as from what you will do; it will have the face that each of you is able and willing to give it. In your hands lies the possibility of a vital renewal that can place our Family among the institutions blessed by God and the Church, fruitful in good works and in new and vigorous shoots, or else condemnation to a progressive barrenness that will end in final extinction.

    No, I do not doubt your response; I know you too well by now. But I cannot set aside my clear duty to call each of you, forcefully and without half-measures, to an awareness of the grave responsibility that rests on those who, like us, in times of such anguished confusion, have received without any particular merit the gift of faith, the life of grace, the joy of conscious participation in the paschal mystery of Christ and, on top of that, the outstanding gift of a religious vocation.

    This is the hour of the most conscious and therefore most decisive and determining choice, for us and for those who will come after us. May the fatherly goodness of God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, through the intercession of Mary Most Holy Immaculate and of her mother and ours, Saint Anne, bring to completion in each of us the work so providentially begun.

    Rome, March 25, 1971

    Feast of the Incarnation of the Word

    Your Mother

    Sr. A. Goffreda Roberto

    Opening Address

    of the Special General Chapter

    Delivered by the Most Reverend Superior General

    Sr. A. Goffreda Roberto

    Rome, September 2, 1969

    My Daughters and Sisters,

    I would have wished that a voice far more authoritative than mine, both by the importance of office and by personal competence (the Most Reverend Father Edward Heston, Secretary of the Sacred Congregation for Religious, had agreed to give the Opening Address, but at the end of August he suddenly had to leave for the United States), might resound in this hall at the opening of our Special Chapter; but since the Lord has disposed otherwise when it was no longer possible to make other suitable arrangements, I hope you will not mind if it is your Mother who addresses to you the first official word of greeting and exhortation.

    First of all, of greeting: welcome, daughters from Italy and America, from Africa and Palestine; I look at you, I recognize each one of you, and the anxiety that cannot help making my heart tremble at this crucial moment for the life of our Institute - however long awaited and prepared - is eased by the confidence your presence inspires in me.

    You too have brought here the weight of your anxieties, your uncertainties, problems and difficulties; but I know that your only aim is to seek God's will for our Institute, in accordance with what the Church of the Council has already wisely laid down regarding religious life in general, and in relation to the needs and demands of the contemporary world.

    All together, then, setting aside every human and particular viewpoint and interest, we will seek to interpret this holy Will of God, drawing it first of all from the Gospel, the fundamental and perennial Code of consecrated life; then from the Council Documents and from the precious spiritual heritage left to us by our venerated Mother Rosa, whose spirit must today more than ever hover among us to guide us and safeguard her Work; and finally from the “signs of the times,” of which each of you must be a faithful and sincere expression in relation to the experience of the particular places, situations, mentalities and needs she has come here to represent.

    We will work together, and Mother Rosa will be among us; and the Spirit of God will enlighten and guide us all the better the more upright our intention and docile our will. The Institute, as our Mother always affirmed, is his Work, and it is he who will make us understand in which direction we must guide it, adapting it to the new times without altering its substantial nature, indeed restoring to it its original vitality. You know well how the Council reaffirmed the esteem the Church has not only for religious life in general but for each Institute in particular, and how much it cares that every Congregation remain faithful to the spirit and purposes proper to its Founder.

    First requirement: unity in truth and charity.

    Our Mother Foundress was a contemplative and an apostle. It can be said of her that she anticipated in the fullest sense what no. 8 of the Decree “Perfectae Caritatis” says about Institutes devoted to apostolic activity. Indeed, Mother Rosa's whole life was permeated with apostolic spirit and all her apostolic action was animated by a religious spirit raised to the high degrees of mystical contemplation.

    These two guiding lines (excluding, of course, mystical contemplation, which is a gift of God and not the creature's choice) must characterize the spirituality of our Institute:

  • a religious spirit that permeates the life of each Sister to the point of turning her every breath into an act of union and offering;

  • apostolic activity marked by total availability to every spiritual or material need of our suffering or needy brothers and sisters, in body or in spirit.

    • On these two guiding lines, docile to the directives of the Church and attentive to the needs of today's world, we must establish the principles for renewing our spirituality and for adapting the structures of the Congregation and of each Work to the demands of the apostolate. We must therefore preserve the constitutive unity of the spirit, yet without in any way sacrificing apostolic needs to a claim of outward uniformity and fixity, today less than ever compatible with the headlong advance of scientific and technical progress and with the unpredictable changeability of the political, social, economic and spiritual conditions of peoples.

    Unity, then, unity, but in the truth of real situations and above all in the charity of mutual understanding; in that charity which must establish among us, as Saint Paul says, “the bond of perfection” and effectively promote the coming of the Kingdom of God. Is this not the ideal to which we have all consecrated our lives?

    Consecrated our lives: ours is indeed a consecrated life, and it belongs to the Lord.

    “Renewal” means greater fidelity

    And it is from this angle, in my view, that we must first of all tackle the problem of renewal.

    In these times of protest, when all values, and first of all moral and spiritual ones, are being called into question, not only by the young or by the laity but also by so many men and women religious, it is necessary that, with the Church of the Council and with the Holy Father, we confirm our fidelity to the bonds that have bound and bind us to God by virtue of religious profession, and proclaim their full moral and juridical force.

    It is true that the Instruction “Renovationis Causam,” issued this year by the Sacred Congregation for Religious, grants Institutes in art. 34 the faculty to replace “temporary vows with bonds of a different kind, such as a promise made to the Institute,” and that this Chapter Assembly, under the same article, will have to decide on the matter; but it must not be forgotten that, first of all, this concerns only temporary vows, and that the following article of the same Instruction specifies: “...this temporary bond leads to the practice of the three evangelical counsels, so as to constitute a true preparation for perpetual profession.” And the following articles go on reaffirming the importance of “single and perpetual” profession. Nor can we pass over in silence the even more explicit statement in no. 44 of “Lumen Gentium”: “the consecration will be the more perfect, the more firm and stable the bonds...”.

    It is clear, therefore, that the Church in no way meant to devalue the sublimity of religious consecration or to lessen the seriousness of the commitment the soul makes directly with God through religious vows. On the contrary, by proclaiming that the religious state “belongs inseparably to the life and holiness of the Church,” the Council proclaimed the need for religious life, in harmony with the new times, to be chosen more consciously and lived in a more personal, more responsible and more consistent way; which certainly does not mean lessening the importance of the Vows, but rather increasing it.

    But the duty of greater awareness and responsibility regarding consecration does not fall only on individual members of the Institute; it obviously concerns even more those who bear, wholly or partly, the burden of its government and direction; and it fully and comprehensively concerns this Chapter Assembly today, which, by virtue of the ordinary laws of the Church and the provisions issued by Pope Paul VI in the Motu Proprio “Ecclesiae Sanctae,” not only holds supreme authority in our Congregation but has the task of establishing the norms on which the new Constitutions will be drafted, which will regulate its life and nourish its spirit in the years to come.

    The cornerstones of religious life

    We must therefore study, in the light of the Council Documents and in particular of “Perfectae Caritatis,” the fundamental principles that must govern the practice of the virtues inherent in the three religious Vows:

  • Chastity, which must be regarded not as a more or less generic renunciation but as an “outstanding gift of grace” and a virtue that “frees the human heart in a unique way so that it may burn ever more with love for God and for all people”.

  • Poverty, which, in both individual and collective practice, must become more honest because more real, more authentic because more effective, so that above all it may be “a sign which can and ought to attract all the members of the Church to an effective and prompt fulfillment of the duties of their Christian vocation”.

    • Let us make sure that from now on certain inaccurate interpretations of this virtue are no longer possible, so that it is no longer confused with a prudent financial skill that encourages saving or, worse still, with a degrading exercise of avarice. May all understand the beauty of this superhuman detachment, to teach us which Christ, “though he was rich, became poor” and made “us rich by his poverty”.

  • No. 14 of “Perfectae Caritatis” has opened a wonderful perspective for our life with its new interpretation of the virtue of religious Obedience: an interpretation that unites superior and subject in practicing the same virtue, both engaged in the common search for God's will according to each one's individual charism. Here too emerges the figure of the divine Model who “came to do the will of the Father” and became obedient to him “unto death on a cross,” and this clarifies better than any other consideration the concept expressed in no. 2 of the same Decree, namely that “the fundamental norm of religious life is the following of Christ as proposed by the Gospel”.

    • The practice of the virtues inherent in the religious Vows must be joined by the very many virtues needed for a well-ordered and serene common life.

    Much has also been clarified regarding the concept of common life. Rightly, precedence has been given to the concept of communion of life and ideals over that of simultaneous timetables and shared practices, something the apostolic commitments from which a religious living in the climate of our time cannot excuse herself always make difficult and sometimes impossible; but this communion of spirits must absolutely be lived, so that the work of a Community, even if carried out at different times, in different places and in different ways, effectively tends toward a single goal and makes use of all the modern criteria of complementarity and subsidiarity that the Superior, in agreement with those responsible for the Works, must use intelligently and prudently. In our time, when the assertion of the rights of the human person prevails or tries to prevail even over the interests of the Community, affecting every social class and every aspect of life, the illusion could easily creep into our world too that a person freed from the ties of the Constitutions and the encumbrances of common life, living in the world, could do greater good than if constrained within religious life and the Works of the Institute.

    Now, while it is unfortunately true on the one hand that the short-sightedness of an ill-prepared Superior and poor organization of work and distribution of tasks could at least partly justify this claim, it is even truer that a Community in which a prudent and far-sighted Superior has given each Sister the task most congenial to her, allowing her to make the best use of her natural gifts and specific training, in a climate where human courtesy and Christian virtue vie with each other to put everyone at ease, can produce, from the human and apostolic point of view, results that could never come from the same number of people working in isolation and independently.

    But Sisters who are humanly and religiously prepared are needed, and Superiors with organizational ability. May our work and sacrifices today prepare such model Communities for a not too distant tomorrow!

    Community life, as religious life lived in a particular Congregation, also imposes particular norms, those commonly called “regular observances.” Renewal cannot and certainly must not abolish them, but it will have to adapt them to the concrete demands of the apostolate and ensure that they help to shape positively the particular “style” of our religious Family, to form wills, and to be themselves a “sign” that edifies and draws others. In a word, the Sisters must be able and know how to give these small or great “observances” an authentic stamp of interiority.

    Second requirement: interiority and consistency

    Interiority. No practice, no action is valid unless it is interiorized, unless it springs from an inner impulse and conviction. In a word, unless the one who acts possesses an inner life of her own made supernaturally valid by union with God. It may be said that this statement is nothing new, since so much has always been said and written about the interior life and union with God; but has it always been properly understood what was meant, and above all have people truly managed to live this life of union with God? Many, yes, certainly, through spontaneous docility to the inner movements of Grace. But today living this interior life is more difficult than ever, for a combination of reasons it would take long to list. I will simply say that today the interior life is possible only on condition that there is sufficient knowledge of revealed religion and solid formation of the will. It follows that the study of religion must today have a much more substantial and solid place and approach in the Sisters' lives than it had in the past. From the point of view of apostolic action too, if until a few years ago knowledge of the Catechism of Pius X could (and I do not know to what extent!) suffice for Sisters working apostolically in a social environment whose cultural level was generally low, today, when the average cultural level has risen considerably and the need for high specialization in every field is increasingly felt, it would be absurd for the Sisters - well known as specialists in the science of God's love - to be ignorant of the subject they are bound to teach, if not always theoretically, at least always practically.

    Nor can one answer, as perhaps was once done, that not everyone is capable of learning; we do not intend to make professional theologians of them, nor does the Church ask so much, but I believe I must affirm that a young woman who is unable to study religious truths in suitable depth cannot today be admitted to religious life. Otherwise we will continue - and not without grave responsibility - to see certain serious inconsistencies persist in our Institute which yesterday's ignorance made, if not excusable, at least explicable. Inconsistencies which lay people, far more perceptive than we perhaps think, and also less generous, notice not without scandal. On the part of many sisters there is no ill will, only invincible ignorance. We cannot, however, allow certain situations to be repeated in new generations of sisters. The Capitulars who will be charged with studying the problems connected with the formation of young sisters will take note of this need.

    But the study of religion is necessary for everyone, including those who are no longer young, if we want them too to share in the hoped-for renewal. For all must live the interior life, and this is not possible without going back to its natural source, which is the deepest possible knowledge of God. For too long “piety” has been spoken of as if it were identical with outward participation in the so-called practices of piety and with the “regular observance” of the Constitutions. Among other things, this is shown by the repetition of the expression “in common” which the Constitutions themselves use regarding meditation, spiritual reading and prayers in general, as if they were nothing but outward acts to be performed in a set way and all together, rather than invisible springs from which the soul must be nourished day by day in divine intimacy.

    By this I certainly do not mean to condemn or despise practices “in common,” but I feel the duty to stress the need for the new Constitutions to give due emphasis to what is the food of the soul, an eminently individual matter, before speaking of things or acts to be done in common. And if we then wish to speak, as we must, of common prayer, we must recall the essentially collective and fundamentally communal value of liturgical prayer, first of all Holy Mass, offered by the whole Community, enlivened by the Grace of the Mystical Body, and directed communally toward God. But even this prayer will have no subjective meaning for Sisters who are not suitably instructed in the Bible and the Liturgy.

    Nor, finally, can personal prayer be neglected, which for a soul of interior life must be as unceasing as breathing.

    Sometimes people complain that many Sisters put prayer to the Saints first in their personal piety. But this is not surprising. They know the Saints, or think they know them, through reading biographies, even those of questionable historical and ascetical value. But unfortunately they know God even less. And so they turn with greater confidence to those they think they know better.

    The interior life is the soul of all fruitful apostolic activity

    There is certainly no need to explain to you how and why the interior life must also be the soul of all apostolic action. Nor that there can be no apostolic activity fruitful and pleasing to God unless it is part of the life of the Church, at whatever level one works. I know you are well convinced of this, not least because the Council Documents are more than explicit on the matter. I will simply remind you, if there were any need, that another essential feature of our apostolic activity must be fidelity to the charism of the origins, that is, to the spirituality and purposes of our Mother Foundress. I would not think it necessary to add anything more on this point, were it not that my anxiety, sharpened by the many difficulties with which I and all my Collaborators must struggle day after day in governing the Institute, obliges me to urge you to make a careful, dispassionate, concrete and realistic study of our Institute's present possibilities in the apostolic field.

    Mother Rosa, in her total dedication to God and to her neighbor in need, and according to the possibilities of her time, did not wish to close, and in fact did not close, her heart and her door to any form of assistance.

    Our possibilities today are extremely limited; and meanwhile, far more peremptorily than a hundred years ago, society asks us to do well the good we profess to do. Certain empirical improvisations, allowed in other times, are today neither conceivable nor possible. Still less are they honest. I entrust to the Chapter Assembly, and especially to those who will be charged with studying and developing the third outline, the proposals to be made and the decisions to be taken. I beg you, however, not to be led astray by sentimental motives or misguided zeal. This is a point that may decide the life or death of our religious Family, and in the short term.

    Another consideration to bear in mind: the apostolic necessity and advisability of accepting the collaboration of lay people wherever possible. This need has been stressed for some time now, but it does not appear to have been understood and accepted by the Sisters everywhere.

    Another aspect of our apostolic action, certainly not negligible, is missionary activity. The Council Decree “Ad Gentes” proclaims the essentially missionary nature of the Church and states that “the work of evangelization is a basic duty of the People of God” (no. 35).

    And it continues: “This sacred Synod invites all to a deep interior renewal, so that, having a vivid awareness of their own responsibility for the spreading of the Gospel, they may do their share in missionary work among the nations.”

    If this invitation is authoritatively addressed by the Council to the whole “People of God,” should we not feel it addressed particularly to us, missionaries by the special charism of our Foundress?

    I hear your answers: we have no personnel! I know that only too well! But does the material impossibility of extending our work of evangelization beyond the boundaries already reached with such effort excuse us from forming within ourselves a more deeply and sincerely missionary soul?

    Note that the Council invites “all the faithful” to evangelize the nations. Can it expect everyone to go to mission lands? Certainly not. It invites all to a deep interior renewal so as to acquire “a vivid awareness of their own responsibility for the spreading of the Gospel.” Now I ask you again: are we all, as we strictly should be, true missionaries in spirit? That is, since we cannot carry out specifically missionary work among unbelievers, do we have the missionary spirit the Council says is a duty for the whole People of God?

    Moreover, are we sufficiently aware of how much the very lands we live in, officially Catholic, need evangelization? In Italy and outside Italy, do our Works have the missionary character suited to the environment we live in, or do they leave something to be desired from that same apostolic point of view?

    Forgive me if I am perhaps too frank, but at times I have had the impression that for many Daughters of Saint Anne the missionary question does not exist at all and has simply been left to those who, by specific vocation or under obedience, have gone to work in mission lands. I recommend to all the reading of nos. 35, 36 and 37 of the Decree “Ad Gentes,” so that you may be convinced that my heartfelt appeal is not the expression of a personal preference of mine but the fulfillment of a duty that so far has seemed to me rather neglected. I then entrust the answer to those who will be particularly charged with studying this question.

    Third requirement: commitment to the formation of young Sisters

    The fact that, besides the sisters elected to the Special Chapter by their respective Provincial Chapters, we judged it advisable to summon to the General Chapter as experts, using a faculty granted by the Motu Proprio, all those who in one way or another could be considered specifically competent or experienced in the formation of young Sisters, shows the particular importance we rightly attach to this most delicate and vitally important area of religious life.

    This importance had already been affirmed by the Decree “Perfectae Caritatis,” which said: “... the up-to-date renewal of institutes depends very largely on the training of their members” (no. 18).

    Now, the Capitulars charged with studying the problems of formation are greatly helped by being able to use, besides the Council Documents, the Instruction of the Sacred Congregation for Religious “Renovationis Causam,” which I have already cited, whose norms, as you surely know, have for us the force of law, albeit on an experimental basis.

    I do not wish to go on at length, having already greatly tried your patience and still having to deal with what is perhaps the most important subject of study, that of government. I will merely recommend to those concerned that they consider the basic principles of formation as presented by the Instruction, and the clear and precise distinction between the various stages of formation and their respective commitments, in particular the Novitiate and the Juniorate. The experiments already made have served above all to make us notice and measure the extreme difficulty of this matter, both in itself and in its necessary application to the psychology and mentality of young women today.

    The problems of government

    And now we come to what I would call the point where all the other problems converge: that of government, considered at every level.

    “All the posts of Superior,” Mother Rosa wrote to a daughter who was perhaps a little faint-hearted, “carry the same weight in every house and every city; the responsibility of that post admits no exception.”

    This is perfectly true. If at the level of general and provincial government the scope of the problems to be solved and the commitments to be met may be daunting, at the level of local government the delicacy and immediate urgency of problems concerning souls and the apostolate, which must be answered without possibility of delay, are perhaps even more pressing. The anguish of a single soul can sometimes reach the breadth of an infinite horizon.

    Let us now start from the widest horizon, central government, and briefly examine the basic problems connected with it.

    a) Decentralization: Let it be quite clear that the Council, while loudly proclaiming the dignity and rights of the human person, in no way intended to destroy or diminish the hierarchical order of the Church and of the Institutions that belong to her. Nevertheless, in the light of the very principles of subsidiarity and complementarity sanctioned by the Council and placed at the foundation of every well-ordered government, that order must be concretely and realistically reconsidered. Hence the problem of decentralization arises.

    Decentralization is required for canonical and juridical reasons and for practical reasons.

    But it is my clear duty to remind you that the greater autonomy and freedom of action the Chapter will grant Provincial and Local Superiors through the new Constitutions must in no way undermine the fundamental unity of spirit. On the contrary, the more independently “superiors at every level, endowed with the appropriate faculties,” can act from now on, and the less “they are obliged to have too frequent recourse to higher authorities” (these are the words of art. 18 of the Motu Proprio “Ecclesiae Sanctae”), the more they must be imbued with the spirituality proper to the Institute, so that there is not only theoretical unity of hearts and ideals but also substantial consistency of direction and concrete purposes, even within the necessary and legitimate variety in applying methods required by the variety of places, traditions, psychology and social conditions in general.

    Without this willing and consistent unity, decentralization would be the beginning of the end of Rosa Gattorno's Work. For how could one recognize, in a disjointed and fragmented Institute, the religious Family to which Mother Rosa gave this counsel: “Pray and love one another all with the same love, and try to reach that beautiful unity of thought and action, so that all together you form one heart and one mind, because you all tend toward one center, which is God”?

    I must therefore urge the Commission that will study the practical implementation of “decentralization” to reflect maturely and to draw up very clear and precise norms to govern relations between the various levels of government.

    Equal attention will be needed in examining the problems connected with administrative decentralization.

    b) Downsizing - If the problem of decentralization raises questions for the Institute's future, that of downsizing presses with anguished immediacy.

    I am certainly revealing no secret in telling you that the shortage of Sisters requires the withdrawal of a considerable number of Communities from their Works. A plan of action already agreed upon between the Generalate and the Provincial Superiors of Italy will be submitted to this Assembly for examination and discussion, since it also provides for a revision of the boundaries of the present Provinces and the erection of new ones.

    It may seem strange at first sight to reduce the number of Houses while planning to increase the number of Provinces, but this second measure is not only a consequence of the coming decentralization, which will place greater commitments and responsibilities on Provincial Superiors, but also, and I would say above all, of the greater awareness that the Council and the times we live in have given us of the delicacy and depth of the needs of each Work and each Sister, which call for ever vigilant and caring attention and plenty of time available for each one.

    Government at the provincial level will take on a new face and renewed features through decentralization and downsizing.

    The Provincial Superior, while respecting the greater autonomy that must also be granted to the government of Communities, must carry out with the utmost solicitude and necessary promptness her task as teacher, guide and animator of works. The Provincial Council too must acquire greater prominence and more defined features, on the model of the structure of the General Council.

    c) The relationship between authority and obedience. I have kept for last what I consider the essential problem, the one which, if it remains unsolved or does not find a truly correct solution in the light of faith and with the strength of good will, will render vain any prudent measure or reform of government.

    I am referring to the fundamental relationship between authority and obedience.

    The new concept of obedience, sanctioned by no. 14 of “Perfectae Caritatis,” rests more on free choice and individual responsibility than on traditional “dependence and submission,” which are more passive and impersonal and much less responsible.

    This new concept, certainly nobler and more in keeping with the dignity of the human person, requires an entirely new approach to human, theological and ascetical formation, which is certainly not easy to impart to those who are no longer young and therefore less responsive to the impulse toward new spiritual orientations, though at the same time also exposed to the easy appeal of a greater autonomy they are not always prepared to exercise.

    Unfortunately, the present crisis of authority, so widely recognized and deplored, is nothing but the genuine revelation of a serious lack of formation: in everyone. In those who exercise authority without adequate preparation and often without human aptitude, and in those who must obey without a deep religious spirit.

    The remedy is not easy. I believe the best method is (and here a most delicate task of re-education by major Superiors comes into play) to begin truly to exercise authority with that “spirit of service” which is basically the key concept of no. 14 of “Perfectae Caritatis.” It will not always be easy, and no immediate fruits will be seen; but I think that as the Sisters come to see the Superior among them as a copy of Jesus, who could say to his disciples, “I am among you as one who serves” (Lk 22:27), they will end up feeling moved to offer superiors that humble deference which can draw meaning and value only from “a spirit of faith and love for God's will”.

    Moreover, those who exercise authority at any level must at last show themselves sincerely detached from office and truly convinced - and demonstrate it in practice - that God's greatest gift is to be a Sister, not to be a Superior. There would be much to say on this point, but I entrust to the good sense of the relevant Commission the task of drawing the appropriate lessons from the answers given on this point by the great majority of Sisters to the questions of the Questionnaire.

    Finally, the authority-obedience relationship must find a suitable solution in its most natural setting, the climate of Community. There is much talk of “family spirit,” but people do not always show in practice that they know how to live it and help others live it. May the new Constitutions give clear, persuasive and effective norms on this point too.

    The revision of the Constitutions: fundamental criteria

    Allow me to say a final word precisely about the criteria by which we must prepare and complete what constitutes, according to the Church's will, the ultimate and essential purpose of our Chapter work: drafting the new text of the Constitutions.

    Our guide in this, besides the general spirit and the suggestions scattered here and there in the Council Documents, will be articles 12, 13 and 14 of the oft-cited Motu Proprio “Ecclesiae Sanctae,” which indicate practically and explicitly the elements that must make up the new Text.

    But let it be quite clear that this is a revision, not a new composition: art. 6 of the same Motu Proprio warns: “This General Chapter has the power to alter, by way of experiment, certain prescriptions of the Constitutions, provided that the purpose, nature and character of the Institute are preserved.”

    Now, I am the first to be convinced that the word “certain,” which in itself might seem rather restrictive, should instead, at least as far as our Constitutions are concerned, be understood and applied quite broadly. For a long time, even well before the Council, those who wished to live their consecration to the full had felt the need for a text of Constitutions that would be a true Code of life, allowing, indeed promoting and fostering, the soul's growth and safeguarding the free flowering of apostolic initiatives, while remaining within the proper limits of religious discipline and general order.

    If our Constitutions did not fully meet these legitimate aspirations, now fully understood and providentially satisfied by the Council, the fault certainly does not lie with the Mother Foundress. We all know what painful and even dramatic events accompanied, one might say step by step, the drafting of our Constitutions, until, in a period of extremely rigid ecclesiastical legalism, they reached the calm harbor of approval by the Holy See, reduced to a prudently anonymous and impersonal tone. But in those Constitutions the great soul and burning charity of the Foundress were as if imprisoned and constrained; let them now be revealed in their fullness, let them blaze forth as she would have wished, as she would certainly do today had she been granted to live this wonderful evangelical springtime on earth.

    But may this springtime the Lord grants us to live in the garden of the Church produce, in the flowerbed entrusted to us, flowers of charity, of understanding for others' weakness, of prudence and patience. I do not mean to quench any enthusiasm, but allow me, against my own temperament and the fervor I feel blazing within me, to fulfill the duty imposed on me by the office the Lord has entrusted to me and the responsibility with which he has invested me.

    Ours is an extremely difficult and delicate task. As things stand in our Congregation, because of the shortage of vocations that has afflicted us for some time, the elderly or at any rate mature members considerably outnumber the young ones.

    This places us in a very strange and contradictory situation. We must, that is, prepare a text of Constitutions that will allow the young women of today and tomorrow to live their religious life in the full expansion of their fresh and exuberant spirituality, yet meanwhile we must try it out (for you know well that everything will have to be tested) with members who, in the great majority, are no longer young, and of many of whom it would be useless and perhaps even cruel and unjust to ask a radical change of mentality and spiritual attitude.

    The Lord could certainly work a miracle. But he lets us act by ordinary ways and with ordinary means, giving us the light we need provided we know how to ask him for it with humility and love. With love above all, because there is no authentic love that does not have humility as its first component. Between yesterday and this morning we have been told by different voices and in different ways that Love is the sum of all the virtues. And the measure of our love for God, needless to say, is the love we have for our neighbor.

    It is certainly not my wish that the young, enthusiastic and generous souls the Lord has given our Family as a precious treasure should become the Galileos of this new Copernican revolution, still less do I wish to halt the providential and irresistible movement of this “revolution.”

    But the “Servant of the Lord,” the Messiah foretold by Isaiah (42:3), was described and characterized as the one who would not break the bruised reed or quench the flickering wick.

    Now, it must be admitted that even in our Family there is no lack of “bruised reeds and flickering wicks.” But if we examine the causes of their condition, we will very rarely find them in conscious and deliberate ill will; for the most part they are deserving sisters, worn out by work borne for decades without reserve or sparing themselves. And if their flame does not give the brilliant light the new times would require, it is because at the time of their youthful formation the means were far fewer and the demands modest. In most cases one could say that their only fault is to have been born too soon.

    You, Daughters and Sisters, who are fortunate to be young in years or have the merit of having kept youth of spirit in the maturity of years, please have the right and proper understanding: would it really seem consistent to you to proclaim the evangelical inspiration of our “renewal” while at the same time carrying out the thoroughly unevangelical work of “breaking the bruised reeds or quenching the flickering wicks”?

    We must therefore avoid both that the young be reduced to immobility and to the consequent inevitable disgust at the inauthenticity of a way of life which, while claiming to be the most genuine fulfillment of the Evangelical Counsels, in fact makes their practice more difficult, and that the elderly fall into discouragement because they are expected to move at a faster pace than they were used to or, worse still, faster than their actual capacities allow. And if it would be both foolish and harmful to clip the young sisters' wings and so jeopardize the Institute's future, it would be equally foolish and harmful, and ungenerous besides, to push to the margins of the Congregation, like useless logs, the elderly sisters who until now have borne, like the Gospel laborers of the first hour, “the burden of the day and the heat” (Mt 20:12).

    It is up to us, then, it is up to each of you, with the help of the Holy Spirit, to work so as to create a harmonious balance between old and new. Someone might tell me that the Gospel says “new wine is not put into old wineskins” (Mt 9:17), but I would answer that this wine is new only in certain respects, while its constituent elements are the unchangeable ones set by God's eternal saving plan. And I could also reply, keeping to the Gospel style, that “every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like the master of a household who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old” (Mt 13:52).

    Indeed, allow me, placed by God like that master of the household as guardian of a common treasure of inestimable value, neither to permit it to be squandered out of a reckless craving for novelty, nor, on the other hand, out of petty fear of damage, to abandon it in the mustiness of a hermetically sealed chest to the voracious tooth of moths.

    I therefore urge on you the greatest wisdom and discretion so that, in the necessary renewal of the Institute, its genuine charismatic character and fundamental unity of spirit may remain intact and indeed shine with new light; but no less respectful and prudent care to create living conditions everywhere suited to the needs of the contemporary world, and to overcome the difficulties arising from the need to adapt the new Constitutions to the human, intellectual and spiritual needs of religious belonging to different nations and continents. Young women raised in different climates, bearing in the unconscious substrate of their psychology and in the awareness of their life experiences the disparate legacies of family, historical and political events and the effects of different social and economic conditions, will be able to find an adequate response to their needs and aspirations and effective help for their human and spiritual growth only in an environment saturated with charity and governed by a code of life permeated by the universal teaching of the Gospel, made concrete and relevant by the motherly catholicity of the Church of Christ.

    The road opening before us is neither short nor easy. And whether the stretch corresponding to the celebration of the Chapter, which I now declare open, proves long or short, calm or somewhat stormy, let us remember that the longest, most delicate and most arduous stretch will be that of gradual implementation.

    We are comforted by the example of the prudent gradualness and humane spirit of accommodation that the Church shows in every decision and, if you like, also by the thought of God's long-suffering patience, who, for all his infinite omnipotence, lets two thousand years go by before humanity, dragged along by its own errors, finds itself for the first time in a decisive face-to-face encounter with the Gospel and begins laboriously to spell out its fundamental lines.

    I do not know how many decades, or centuries, or even millennia it will take for humanity to decipher fully and at last to live Jesus' liberating message. But I know for certain, and it is my duty to remind you, that God has called us to occupy in the Church, and with the Church in humanity, a vanguard position laden with responsibility.

Opening Address

of the 2nd Session

of the Special General Chapter

Delivered by the Most Reverend Superior General

Sr. A. Goffreda Roberto

Rome, September 4, 1970

My dearest sisters and daughters,

it is certainly not my intention to retrace the guidelines of the Special Chapter set out in the opening address of the first session.

But I must point out that, whereas then I invited you to consider and study the various aspects of religious life from a rather general point of view, as was obvious and necessary for a first overall look, today I invite you to rethink in depth the essential elements of the specific spirituality of the Daughters of Saint Anne.

Now, that is, we must strive to understand deeply the charism of our Foundress and therefore what the Lord continues to ask of us through meditation on her teachings and generous imitation of her way of life: of us collectively, as a religious Family, and of each of us individually, as a person consecrated to him.

In the three days just past, sublime truths have been taught or recalled to us. Truths that must not remain at the level of theoretical knowledge but must be translated into dispositions of spirit and ways of behaving.

As this second and final session of the Special Chapter opens, we must prepare ourselves to undertake, we first of all, an ascent toward spiritual heights that may make the head spin for those more used to clinging firmly to the ground, but which promise the discovery of horizons so fascinating that it is worth the attempt.

We cannot measure by ourselves the level of holiness we are capable of reaching, nor is there, I believe, a fixed limit given us to know; but we can and must place ourselves in an attitude of absolute availability. It would be unworthy hypocrisy to prepare to load our Sisters with burdens that we ourselves “are not willing to lift a finger to move”; but it would also be shameful cowardice to mark out a path of mediocrity and lukewarmness for fear of the burden we too will have to carry.

We must not, then, measure the burden by our human strength alone but entrust ourselves to the Lord, who “gives what he commands and commands what he has given,” in Saint Augustine's incisive phrase.

We have been told in these days that the results of our work will set the course our Congregation will follow for the next 50 years. But I tell you that if the results of this Chapter of ours are not what they must be at so decisive an hour, they may bring about the end of our Institute within a much shorter time.

Already at the end of the first session we had been invited to consider, in the unequivocal terms of figures and percentages, our serious numerical situation.

I cannot tell you, unfortunately, that the situation has improved in the meantime. I can state that it has worsened, as was foreseen.

And yet our pressing problem of quantity cannot be solved in corresponding terms of quantity, but only in terms of quality. In other words, if we want to save the Institute and obtain from God the number of vocations needed for its survival in the Church, we who are more aware must show all our Sisters the place our Congregation holds in God's plan revealed to the Foundress, and begin ourselves to carry out this plan, at once, with full generosity, with unreserved availability, whatever the cost.

The first session of our Chapter, simply because a second was almost certainly expected, could leave room for some convenient escape. Someone might protest, with how much genuine humility I do not know, “Let the others do it, they are more capable; I am not able,” or the whole Assembly might, even with the most honest intentions, put off to the second session whatever was more troublesome, more problematic, less certain of solution and therefore in need of more mature reflection.

Not now! Our duty has now become impossible to postpone, and each one's responsibility leaves no way out.

I am not laying out programs for you. I invite you to abandon yourselves to the prompting of the Spirit, who will act infallibly in us if we open ourselves humbly and trustingly to him.

We will need to read, reflect and discuss; but above all we will need to pray and live in a spirit of faith, hope and charity. May this Chapter mark for each of us the beginning of a more determined and willing drive toward holiness. The rest the Lord will do, as he did for Mother Rosa.

But we cannot think of drawing up a program of holiness while we go on living in mediocrity. Nor, I repeat, can the Constitutions we prepare be such that whoever lives them might fail to become holy. That would be a contradiction the Church could not accept.

With great motherly confidence, wishing each of you serene and fruitful work and invoking God's blessings upon the whole Assembly, I declare the 2nd session of our Special Chapter open.

Address

Delivered by the Most Reverend Mother Sr. A. Goffreda Roberto at the close of the 2nd and final Session of the Special General Chapter: January 26, 1971

My sisters and daughters,

And we have reached the end! An end that at some moments of our long work may have seemed so far away and at some points perhaps so difficult to reach... but we have arrived, and today I feel able to affirm with greater certainty than ever that the Lord has truly been with us day by day, and that day by day there has been with us, invisible but concrete and effective, the motherly presence of Saint Anne, the protection of Mary Most Holy, the inspiration of Mother Rosa and of all the good souls who with her labored and suffered for the founding, consolidation and spread of our religious Family. It is truly consoling to be able to say how concretely we have felt, all these months, this intense communion with those who have gone before us into the heavenly Church but continue to guide and protect us on our earthly pilgrimage.

Help me, therefore, to give thanks to God and his Saints; it is our first duty.

And after God, it is to you that I feel the need and duty to say thank you. On my own behalf and on behalf of the whole Institute. Thank you for the dedication, patience, diligence and love with which each of you carried out the part of the work entrusted to her.

At this point there are so many things I would like to tell you; but let me tell you just one, because I consider it of the utmost importance and therefore want it to stay firmly impressed on your minds and consciences.

You are about to return to your Houses, where you are certainly awaited with anxiety, impatience and, let us admit it, a good dose of curiosity; there are indeed many things the Sisters would like to know, and not without reason, since in a sense what is at stake is the shape of their lives. And you will have to say something!

But remember: what will really count will not be so much what you say as what you show of yourselves in your behavior as you begin again to live beside them, in work and in everyday life.

What you say will certainly also be very important, but it will bear good fruit only if you keep to the suggestions I intend to give you. In truth, it is less a suggestion than a request I am making; a request I make with all the affection of my heart, desiring only the common good, but also, if you will allow me, with all the authority which certainly does not come from my personal qualities but from the heavy weight of responsibility I feel resting on my shoulders toward the whole Congregation.

Your Communities are waiting for you, I said, and waiting with legitimate curiosity; well then, at this more than ever delicate moment, before the official Acts of our Chapter can be published, rather than being bearers of stimulating news, try to be witnesses to a new spirit, that spirit which we have so anxiously sought to rediscover and make vitally our own in these months of prayer and meditation, research and study. This spirit is now set down in the Basic Documents, which represent the most important and definitive part of the Chapter's work; all our Sisters must be able to approach these Documents with full and serene confidence.

During the work, in the discussions that necessarily had to precede choices and decisions, there was some disagreement among us; and it was right that there should be, even if the basic reason for the disagreement was not always expressed with all the clarity I would have wished. In any case, disagreement is legitimate, indeed necessary, and I will certainly not be the one to regret it.

But do not be offended if, in the name of peace of souls, which must be safeguarded at all costs, I remind you at this moment of your responsibility toward the Congregation and especially toward those Sisters whose trust made each of you the interpreter of their thoughts and aspirations. You know well that it is not the opinions of individual Capitulars but the collegial decisions taken by the Assembly that have binding force for all. It follows that if any of you, in her heart, did not feel and still does not feel convinced of the reason for or the advisability of a decision, she is not thereby entitled to reject it; still less will she be allowed, in conversation or discussion, on hearing, as may easily happen, a reservation or criticism from those who did not take part in the Chapter or even from outsiders to the Institute, to try to excuse herself or lessen her own responsibility by saying, “In fact I did not agree” or, worse still, “I voted against it,” or “I spoke but was not listened to,” and the like.

I understand very well that some norms, both among those confirmed and among those added, may easily seem harsh or restrictive to those who perhaps imagined that the Chapter was meant to make religious life easier and more comfortable rather than more like the life of the One who taught us the way to heaven by taking up the cross on his own shoulders first and asking us to follow him more closely. And I also understand that not everyone, until sufficiently enlightened, will manage to grasp that the new norms must be placed in a new context, that of the Second Vatican Council, expressed in the Basic Documents.

I understand, and therefore very willingly make allowance for, the inevitable first impressions that are not entirely positive, at least on certain points. That is, on the part of those who did not take part in the Chapter and could not follow its logical development. But not on your part: if only because of that fundamental spirit of Faith in the presence of the Holy Spirit, whom we constantly invoked as Inspirer and guide of our every decision, and who cannot have allowed our sincere good faith and upright intention to be vitiated in their practical conclusions by serious errors or injustices truly harmful to the Institute.

Please understand me well, however: I do not intend by this to do violence to your consciences by trying to induce an inner assent that you may not feel and to which you are not bound. I ask you only to measure with the yardstick of prudence and charity the words you speak, so that none of you may, even involuntarily and thoughtlessly, cause disorientation or distrust in the souls of the Sisters who have waited, hoped and prayed so much; some, as you well know, have even suffered and offered their lives for the Chapter's success. And we have felt the power of these generous self-offerings.

I ask you only this: be faithful to the Spirit. And you certainly will be if you strive to return to your Communities and your work bearing on your face the features that our whole Family will have to have once it has had the opportunity and time to know, understand and live our spirituality.

On the other hand, you must not forget what has been repeated so often, namely that none of the decisions taken should be considered absolutely final. The norms now approved are only the first step on a path of experimentation that will last for years and will certainly have to undergo changes as errors of judgment, oversights or omissions come to light. From now on we must humbly accept all future corrections and trust in the wisdom of those who will have to take up our work again and adapt it to the process of transformation that is so rapidly changing the face of the world.

Nor would it have been wise to claim to foresee or even forestall everything; every adaptation, if it is not to cause confusion and disorder, must be gradual. We do not claim to have done perfect work. But we think we are not presumptuous in saying that we did our best to complete a task that was not easy in itself and for which none of us was specifically trained.

We entrusted ourselves to the Lord and the Lord answered; and to the poverty of our means, our inexperience and our ignorance, but also to our immense desire to do his Will as expressed to us by the Church, he gave the ability to begin discovering the face of our Institute, as he willed it when he inspired its first design in Mother Rosa and gave Father Tornatore the light to clarify its lines and define its character.

Leaving the Chapter, we are only at the beginning of the road that must lead the Institute to full renewal. I have said and repeated countless times, not only to you but to all the Daughters, that the beginning and end of true renewal lies in the conversion of each of us. And woe to us if we, of all people, did not show that while we strove to trace the theoretical lines of general renewal we worked with even greater commitment for our personal renewal; if we did not show that, while perhaps we have not become wiser, we have truly striven to become better, humbler and more consciously grateful to the Lord for the immense gift of a religious vocation.

Try, then, to make it understood with patient love that the importance of the Chapter's work lies not in this or that norm, nor even in the norms taken as a whole, but in the Basic Documents, in which our most genuine spirituality has been expressed. Help them understand that the norms are only a pointer, a suggestion, a push toward that constant and personal attitude of generosity each must adopt toward the Lord from whom she has received so much. Try to help them see that rather than arguing about the material advisability of certain prescriptions taken in isolation, one must strive to understand the spiritual reason from which they arose and which makes them reasonable and just. And that the norms themselves are not complete, because we did not want them complete, and for good reason. We allowed them to be spare and fragmentary, provided they were reduced to the minimum that could not be postponed, which the immediate good of the Institute required.

Experience will show what remains to be done. And if uncertainties and doubts arise, we will gladly try to explain and shed light. This is the immediate commitment of all of us. But let the Sisters have confidence; they will have it if you show first that you have it, in keeping with the new spirituality we have discovered as the soul of our religious Family. A new spirituality, but an ancient faith: hence the need for an attitude of deep balance and great humility for all.

The Church did not tell us, “go on doing as you have done so far,” but neither did she say, “trust yourselves to your own or others' arbitrary improvisation, outside the furrows of the Magisterium.” The Church told us, “Return to the sources.” To the sources of Christian life, to the sources of our original spirituality. And not only did she tell us so, but she courageously and honestly gave us the example in the Second Vatican Council. So much so that where she recognized that the evangelical spirit had weakened, she confessed it and sought the remedy.

So must we do. At times it may be painful, even sorrowful, perhaps humiliating, to adapt to new orientations and give up a mentality that for decades, in complete good faith, had remained attached to methods and prescriptions that seemed sacred and unchangeable. Just as it may be painful for others to slow down a pace they would instinctively like to be freer and faster.

Let us look to the Church; to the Church that Christ willed to be embodied first of all in Peter, to whom alone he gave the power to “strengthen the brethren.” And tomorrow we will be at the feet of this Rock and will receive, as the Lord's last gift for this Chapter of ours, the word of the Holy Father. I do not know what he will say to us, but I know for certain that the Lord will speak to us through his mouth and that his words must be for us a sacred deposit of truth and a precise program of action.

At the feet of a Pontiff our Mother Rosa made the firm resolution, though heart-rending for her: “I want to do God's will.” Tomorrow, at the feet of the Pontiff, each of us must renew the resolution, certainly less painful but just as firm: to do God's will, whatever the cost.

The Blessing of the Vicar of Christ will seal a period now closing and will be the unfailing assurance of divine help for all that still awaits us. But at that moment we must not stand alone before the Pope; we must carry all our Sisters in our hearts: the sorrows, anxieties and hopes, and also the weaknesses and miseries, ours and theirs; the good will and resolve of all to be what the Holy Spirit, through Mother Rosa, has asked us to be. Above all, to be a sign of that fraternal communion which, in Mother Rosa's words, must be “the coat of arms of the Family of Saint Anne.”

And here is my last request. At the end of 1969 I wished that 1970 might be the year of Faith for our Institute. I felt the need for it precisely so that we might all prepare to seek and recognize, in Faith, the signs of God's will in the life of each and all. Now, at the beginning of 1971, I ask you, and in you I ask all the Daughters of Saint Anne, all the dearest daughters the Holy Mother entrusts to me today: let 1971 be the year of fraternal love, the year in which in our Communities we will strive to live in its fullest meaning that evangelical life of which Mother Rosa gave us so shining an example. And you must show the way to the Sisters who are waiting for you.

With this great hope I offer you my motherly greeting and wish you much serenity and fruitfulness in your work as, in the name of the Lord, I declare closed the second and final Session of the Special General Chapter of our Institute.

“Every renewal of the Church essentially consists in an increase of fidelity to her own calling” (U.R. 6).

The renewal of religious life, too, is nothing other than an act of renewed fidelity to one's specific vocation; for us, to our vocation as Daughters of Saint Anne.

Our renewal does not consist, then, in doing something absolutely new, but in a deeper study of Mother Rosa's original inspiration and a clearer definition of the essential lines of her charism, in order to give our Institute, with a new vital impulse, the possibility of fully embodying its vocation in the present historical moment. Unchanging fidelity to the origins, in the gradual adaptation of our spirituality to the changing conditions of places and times.

The various documents of our origins show that Mother Rosa too discovered and understood only gradually the Spirit's message regarding the specific character the Institute was to have.

At first, scrutinizing the “signs” of her time and considering the neglect suffered by the poorer classes, Rosa simply thought of a work that would respond concretely to these needs, but lacking any defined spiritual character other than that of a Christian charity lived and practiced with great generosity:

“These daughters,” we read in an autograph draft of hers from 1864, “are to work for the increase of our holy Faith and for the care of the sick in their homes; and they will also take in girls at risk, whom they will teach Christian doctrine and needlework.”

Because of Rosa Gattorno's filial devotion to Mary Immaculate (a devotion strengthened and made more relevant than ever by the then recent proclamation of the Dogma of the Immaculate Conception), this not yet clearly defined Society or religious Family would take the name “Daughters of Mary Immaculate,” to which was added “Minims of Saint Francis of Assisi,” since Rosa saw in this Saint the purest and most complete embodiment of her lofty ideal of evangelical poverty.

Saint Anne is entirely absent from Rosa Gattorno's thinking, as indeed is any real spiritual orientation shaped by a particular theological and ascetical content. Charity, and nothing but charity, expressed in a passionate love for the poor and the suffering, in whom she saw and venerated the most faithful image of Christ Crucified, was Rosa's whole program.

The fatherly but firm voice of her spiritual Director first, then the authoritative voice of her Archbishop, would give Rosa the first push toward a more precise definition and above all would firmly require her to give a more concrete answer to what was a simple inner imperative. Caught then in the vise of two equally strong and painfully conflicting obediences, Rosa would ask the Supreme Pontiff to resolve her drama of human motherhood and divine will; and she would receive from the Pontiff the decisive impulse for an undertaking whose turns and developments no one could yet foresee: for example, the founding of the Work in Piacenza rather than in Genoa.

But it is precisely in Piacenza that Saint Anne awaited her, for an encounter that seemed casual at first sight but was in reality decisive and determining, both for Rosa Gattorno's life and for the spiritual direction of her work: for it is to Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore, of the Priests of the Mission, professor of theology at the “Alberoni” College in Piacenza, and already unknowingly the bearer of part of Mother Rosa's charism, that we owe its fundamental clarification and its definitive direction.

The clear “signs” of the divine will, confirming Father Tornatore's advice, led Mother Rosa to place her newborn Congregation under the protection of the mother of Mary Immaculate, Saint Anne; and Saint Anne would be the Bearer of a particular divine message from which the original inspiration of 1864 would draw not only the strength for rapid and effective realization but also, and above all, the light to identify the distinctive character and specific task the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne was to have in the Church.

These, in brief, are the historical facts that the Assembly of Capitulars, wholly intent on seeking the most genuine interpretation of Mother Rosa's charism, drew from the documents of the origins; and it was in this search that it came upon a figure who until now, unfortunately, had remained unjustly in the shadows: that of Father G.B. Tornatore, whose Work “Common Rules of the Daughters of Saint Anne,” written in 1869, is the purest and most precious source of our spirituality.

Therefore today, with devout and moved hearts, the Chapter Assembly feels the duty to affirm that God made use of these two great and generous souls, Mother Rosa Gattorno and Father G.B. Tornatore, to give our Institute that wonderful spiritual wealth which, more than a hundred years later, proves fully relevant and in complete harmony with the perennial teaching of Sacred Scripture and the doctrine of the Second Vatican Council.

The threefold ideal - evangelical poverty, family life and apostolic ardor - that inspired the vision of 1864 finds its definitive development in the spirituality of Saint Anne, which takes concrete form in waiting in poverty of spirit, and motherly dedication.

  • The Spirit of poverty,

    • Understood already by Mother Rosa not only as poverty of material goods but also, and above all, as self-stripping in order to welcome God, it is expressed in all its fullness in the Rule of 1869. Mother Rosa herself judged it so: “... no Rule leads to such lofty sublimity of perfection in humility as this one. Take poverty, and see to what sublimity it is carried: we have nothing, and everything can be taken from us...” (Conference to the Sisters of Sampierdarena, 1870).

    Humility and poverty are therefore, for Mother Rosa, the cornerstones of the spirituality of the Daughters of Saint Anne; humility and poverty are the common denominator of the seven virtues in which, according to the Rule of 1869, the spirituality of our Institute is summed up; humility and poverty are, according to Sacred Scripture, the essential virtues that determine the attitude of the “poor of Yahweh,” among whom we cannot fail to place Saint Anne, mother of Mary and our mother by divine will:

    “So far I have taught you the virtues that make up my spirit... All my actions were animated by lively faith, firm hope, ardent charity, dovelike simplicity, enlightened prudence, deep humility and meekness. And if you are my daughter, in begetting you I can give you no other life than the spirit of these virtues, which is my very life” (Rule of 1869, Chap. II).
