    A brief commentary is enough to show how the spirit of poverty perfectly sums up these seven virtues:

  • “Faith

    • Rests on the word of God... and the Word of God leads infallibly to happiness those who trust in it” (ibid.). To rest on and trust in God's word are two attitudes that necessarily imply poverty and humility: the divine message is revealed only to the poor and the little ones, because only they are ready to welcome it; the proud are incapable of believing: “How can you believe... when you do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (Jn 5:44). “I thank you, Father... because you have hidden these things from the wise and the intelligent and have revealed them to infants” (Mt 11:25; Lk 10:21).

    The “poor of Yahweh” had faith in God's Word: “Surely God is my salvation; I will trust and will not be afraid, for the Lord is my strength and my song” (Is 12:2). Thus the Rule of 1869 sums up the teaching of the Old Testament, which reveals the spiritual riches of poverty, and of the New, which recognizes the truly poor as the privileged heirs of God's kingdom (Cf. Mt 5:3).

    It is also noteworthy that the Rule of 1869 presents Mary at the moment of the Incarnation of the Word as the model of faith, that is, the Gospel passage which, as all now recognize, represents the decisive historical moment in which the spirit of the Poor of the Old Testament, summed up in Mary, abandons itself to God in a supreme act of faith in the fulfillment of the Promise.

  • Hope,

    • In the Rule of 1869 it is identified with the joyful certainty of one who has God as her only treasure and seeks nothing but Jesus Christ and his grace. And therefore she “lives without anxiety about earthly goods and bodily health, leaving to God the care of all these things” (Rule 1869, II), in an attitude inspired by that of Abraham, “who hoped against hope” (Cf. Rom 4:18):

    “... you will always live like a little child in the arms of the heavenly Father, so that you will never lack anything that would be truly good for you and no harm will ever touch you; and this will be so even when at some moment it might seem to you, and to others too, that all was lost.”

  • Charity

    • It is presented in its twofold dimension of love of God and of neighbor: it consists, that is, in seeking God's pleasure in everything, as “Jesus Christ taught us with those words of his: I always do what pleases my Father.”

    And... “just as what God loves most in you is that zeal to give him every pleasure... so this same thing is what he loves most in your neighbors; and therefore you will love your neighbors with the purest charity by wanting and seeking for them that they set their hearts on seeking in everything and always the delight of the heavenly Father.”

    Now, such total availability to God's Will, leading one to imitate Jesus Christ who “always did what pleased the Father,” presupposes a deep spirit of poverty, because only one who is poor in spirit is aware that in Love it is God who takes the initiative; and so, feeling loved by him, she strives to please him by doing his divine will and recognizing in all that happens a message and a proof of love.

  • Simplicity and prudence

    • They are virtues inseparable from inner poverty; “God gladly speaks with the simple who have no duplicity in their hearts,” says the Rule of '69; and it continues: “Let everything in you be light...; in all your actions aim at nothing but your true treasure, which is the pleasure of your God, and then he will gladly converse intimately with you.”

    And with full consistency it shows the necessary relationship between simplicity and prudence: “Simplicity cannot live without the company of prudence,” since “prudence is the light that, between two things, always makes you choose the one that best leads you to acquire and increase the only solid wealth, namely the love of God.”

  • Humility

    • “It is the road to the exaltation that comes from God.” This definition contains all the richness of the biblical tradition and closely echoes the canticle of the Virgin of Nazareth. But what does humility consist in? “... it is a sincere confession, a confession made with love, that the creature has no merit before God...”. Here is the authentic spirituality of the poor, the foundation of their attitude before God, the secret of their total openness to faith and hope; an openness that found its highest expression in Mary and that Jesus Christ raised to the sublime in a total self-emptying that culminated in death on the cross. “Therefore God highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name...” (Phil 2:9).

  • Meekness

    • It is the virtue that excludes any desire to dominate things or persons, in imitation of Christ, the Lamb of God; associated with him in the paschal mystery, we become heirs of his promise: “Blessed are the meek - and the meek are poor by choice - for they will inherit the earth” (Mt 5:5).

    And the Rule of 1869 comments: “My daughters are called to possess the land of human hearts, to cultivate them so that they may bear the fruits for which they were created, namely the fruits of divine love and of all the other Christian virtues.”

    And finally, in the Rule of 1869 the three vows too have a liberating function and guide the Daughter of Saint Anne toward that attitude of spiritual poverty which makes it possible to acquire and deepen the seven virtues listed above:

    “... the three holy virtues of which you take vows are like the body through which and in which the seven virtues live... these being its spirit... Whenever, to reach the fullness of this spirit, you have detached yourself from possessions through holy Poverty, from the pleasures of the flesh through holy Chastity, modesty and detachment from relatives, and from yourself through holy Obedience...”

    “Then you will have offered in yourself a sacrifice of honor, praise and thanksgiving to the Most Holy Trinity...”

    “... but the Lord wishes to lead you to this most lofty holiness in my house and under my motherly guidance, so that you may also be fruitful in holiness in your neighbors...”.

    These passages, taken from the next-to-last Chapter of the Rule of 1869, truly sum up all the essential themes of the vocation of the Daughters of Saint Anne and explain the extraordinary richness of their Foundress's interior life, which was a life of:

    1 - total consecration, in which the virtues inherent in the three religious vows truly form the load-bearing structures (“the body”) of the “interior castle,” where, in a new evangelical dimension, those virtues converge and harmonize which already in the Old Testament shone with the light of holiness in the poor and humble who trustingly awaited the fulfillment of the Promise; among them, Saint Anne.

    2 - consecration grounded in a complete theological plan, in which the initially eminently Christ-centered orientation of Rosa's interior life rises to the heights of the Trinitarian dogma. Mother Rosa, model of the Daughters of Saint Anne, truly made of herself and her life a “sacrifice of honor, praise and thanksgiving to the Most Holy Trinity...”.

    And all this “under the motherly guidance of Saint Anne.” This explains the specific structure of the Congregation, which rests on family spirit in order to be directed toward an eminently apostolic activity.

    II. Family life was to be the life of Rosa Gattorno's “daughters,” already in the very first drafts of a rule; not for nothing was the Foundress a mother.

    This fundamental “family spirit” would take definitive and specific shape under the “motherly guidance” of Saint Anne, honored with the most blessed of motherhoods after that of Mary Most Holy.

    Saint Anne's presence in our Congregation thus remains the symbol of motherhood: “My Institute is nothing but an extension of my Family: God has raised you up so that in you, blessed ones, we may continue to live: I, your mother; Joachim and Mary Immaculate” (Chap. X, 1).

    Here are the specifications deriving from this premise concerning mutual relationships:

    - the relationship between superior and sister will be like that of mother and daughter: “... you will look upon her as your mother.” And how often in her countless letters Mother Rosa would remind Superiors of their duty to be true mothers to the sisters!

    - the relationship among the Sisters: fraternal love must be “the coat of arms of the Family of Saint Anne,” precisely because “all are daughters of one and the same Mother.”

    This same “family spirit,” with an entirely motherly emphasis, will be the soul of the:

    III. Apostolic activity of the Daughters of Saint Anne, an aspect of their vocation inseparable from that of their consecration.

    The Rule of 1869 clearly expresses this need for motherly sensitivity and dedication that must characterize the apostolic and charitable style of the Daughter of Saint Anne:

    “You must regard yourself as the mother of the poor sick; you will love them with a motherly love, pray for them and weep over their spiritual and temporal ills” (Chap. VIII, 3).

    And toward the girls: “... in particular you will show yourself truly a mother to them in their illnesses” (Chap. XIV, 2).

    This brief look at the purpose, spirituality and characteristics of our Institute has tried to sum up the message God wished to entrust to us in placing the figure of Saint Anne in our lives: a message of hope and expectation; no longer, of course, expectation of the coming of the historical Christ, but trusting expectation of the definitive coming of the glorious Christ, which we must live with a joyfully poor heart, so as to be a “sign” of hope for our brothers and sisters.

    Mother Rosa is our model. Her life appears to us as the existential and dynamic embodiment of this wonderful spirituality centered on poverty of spirit; entirely detached from herself, she knew how, with complete simplicity, to identify with her “Crucified Good,” that is, with the highest expression of Christ's voluntary poverty, and at the same time to give herself with a mother's tenderness to God's Work, which she enlivened and made fruitful with her sacrifices.

    Another characteristic easily inferred both from Mother Rosa's spirituality and from the number and variety of the Works she founded is that our religious Family was not willed by God to carry out a single specific work, but must be present in the Church with an attitude of total availability to the changing needs of places and times, and must therefore safeguard and strengthen its distinctive adaptability, raising its tone and nourishing our vocation as apostles at its pure Source:

    “... blessed are you when you can say: I am dying because I wore myself out too much in works of charity” (Mother Rosa, Threads of Gold).

B) The vows

12. The vows of chastity, poverty and obedience are the constitutive elements of consecration and the foundation of religious life as a stable condition of life, shaped for each person by the specific spirituality of the Congregation in which they are professed.

Although they represent the institutionalization of a particular way of life, they do not in themselves exhaust the deep meaning of consecration, which draws its full vigor from the inwardness of the relationship each religious establishes with God through practicing the virtues inherent in the vows and from the sincerity with which he commits himself to fulfilling the obligations that derive from them.

Freely and consciously pronounced, the Vows constitute a moral obligation that draws its force from the Gospel. It is Jesus who presents the Counsels as a stable way of living modeled on his own life.

13. Of chastity alone, however, does Jesus speak as a free choice made “for the sake of the Kingdom of Heaven”201. “Poverty of spirit” is an element of the beatitude proposed to all as a value of liberation and progress, reinforced moreover by the warnings uttered, by way of contrast, against the rich202; and as for obedience, Jesus does not even give an explicit “counsel,” yet he repeatedly proclaims it as the cause of his incarnation, his earthly life and his death203, just as the resurrection is the glory that follows his having “emptied himself” in obedience to the Father “unto death on a cross”204. It would therefore be inconceivable, as well as impossible by the very nature of the human person, to have a life marked by the “sequela Christi” and not characterized by obedience.

Chastity, poverty and obedience, together with common life, are therefore the typical elements of religious life.

Through them, in fact, “the faithful one... gives himself totally to God, loved beyond all things, so that he is ordained by a new and special title to the service and honor of God,” to whom he had already been consecrated by baptism, since by the vows pronounced in the Church he frees himself “from those obstacles which might draw him away from the fervor of charity and the perfection of divine worship” and is joined “in a special way... to the Church and her mystery”205; that is, he commits himself wholly to cooperating in the redeeming mission of Christ living in the visible Church.

Reciprocity of the religious virtues.

14. The relationship among the virtues of chastity, poverty and obedience expressed by the corresponding vows is not one of mere juxtaposition but of harmonious and indispensable complementarity. Each requires and at the same time completes the others.

Strictly speaking, chastity can be called the qualifying element of religious consecration, since it is this virtue that involves a permanent and decisive choice; this is how Christ himself presented it. But on the other hand it can also be said that poverty of spirit is the first and indispensable condition for following Christ in sincere imitation of his sentiments, even before his very way of life: “Let the same mind be in you that was in Christ Jesus,” says Saint Paul, referring to the supreme self-impoverishment of a God who becomes man. And as for obedience, it can be said to be absolutely inseparable from poverty of spirit, of which it is the most authentic and profound expression: it costs less, in fact, to strip oneself of material goods than to renounce the most intimate and personal of goods, the judgment of the intellect and the free decision of the will.206207208

In conclusion, poverty and obedience, understood in the Gospel sense and sincerely practiced, spring from baptismal grace as a concrete expression of the theological virtues and constitute the authentic mark of Christian life. The creature's acceptance of this gift entails total belonging to the Lord, immediate and exclusive adherence to his will, and at the same time gives her the strength to live freely and joyfully in a way different from that of others.

2. The gift of virginity, freely accepted by the creature and sanctioned by the Church through the publicly pronounced vow, “recalls to the minds of all the faithful that wonderful marriage made by God, which will be fully manifested in the future age, in which the Church takes Christ as her only Spouse”213.

Virginity therefore has a particular value as witness:

a) of the love of God, who “so loved humanity that he gave his only Son... that the world might be saved through him”214.

And since many people are unaware of or have forgotten this reality, God chooses persons who make explicit profession of bearing witness to his love, expressing it with a universality opposed to the exclusive character of married love and with a disinterestedness opposed to the demand for reciprocity underlying every human relationship, whether affective or practical. The virgin heart loves God for his own sake and people in him and for him215, but with the same disposition as Christ, whose follower and imitator it is, that is, to the point of being ready to die for them216. b) of the “heavenly goods already present in this world” and “of the new and eternal life won by the redemption of Christ”217.

b) of the life to come

The virgin, in the provisional nature of her state of life, free of any stable tie and solely “anxious about the affairs of the Lord”218, experiences and bears witness already on this earth to the condition of the blessed in heaven, where “they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels”219.

c) God wants people to love one another as brothers and sisters220.

Through virginity, which draws its motive from love and is directed toward love, the religious, intimately united to God by an exclusive bond, draws from him the capacity for a universal love that places her entirely at the service of her brothers and sisters, in a disposition of loving and complete participation in the work of Redemption that Christ continues to accomplish in his Church.

7. This dynamic expansion, however, is possible only on condition of a constant effort at self-transcendence, all the more fruitful the more attentive one is to keeping the heart open and available to the promptings of the Spirit.

Fundamental human qualities are also necessary, and in particular a sound psychological balance, without which it does not seem possible to reach the degree of affective maturity needed to make use of the heart's natural needs and of the maternal instinct itself without stifling them, raising them to a supernatural plane that makes love self-giving and dedication more effective, centering their object on God alone.

Only in this way can chastity chosen “with mature deliberation and magnanimity”226 truly become a “good for the integral development” of the consecrated person227.

8. An important element in achieving this affective maturity is also adequate information about the reality of one's own physical and psychological being; this involves:

- serene and respectful acceptance of the reality of one's body and of the value and limits of one's femininity;

- an objective assessment of one's gifts and limitations;

- and finally both “a suitable knowledge of the duties and dignity of Christian marriage” and an understanding of “the superiority of virginity consecrated to Christ”229.

So that the religious, having understood that while Christian marriage is a “sign” in time of Christ's love for his Church, consecrated virginity is the free gift of an undivided union with Christ for time and eternity, may more easily find the strength to free herself from every human tie and to spread herself joyfully in a dedication that reaches all who need help and comfort without being exhausted in any one of them.

In relation to her specific apostolate too, open to such vast and varied fields, the Daughter of Saint Anne needs proper knowledge of the problems connected with sexuality and a positive view of God's plan, within a context of serene inner balance, so that where necessary she can enlighten consciences or dispel doubts with a competence marked by easy and humble simplicity.

In today's historical and social context, the explosion of hedonistic and even blatantly sensual tendencies characterizing every sector of life constitutes an objective danger for chastity, added to the subjective dangers present in every age: exuberant imagination, exaggerated emotionalism, inner imbalance caused by poor health or excessive fatigue.

The dynamism of modern life also requires the Sisters to have frequent or habitual contact with lay people whose mentality differs from the religious one or is entirely anti-Christian; nor should we underestimate the influence of the enormous spread of the media of social communication, which have now penetrated every environment, with their positive and negative contributions.

10. The lack of a serene family atmosphere in the community creates a situation that heightens the dangers to chastity, if it does not create new ones. Primacy of Charity.

11. Ultimately, virginity of heart and body represents the triumph of Charity in the life of a woman who, having become God's exclusive possession, turns to others to bear witness to divine love before all and translate it into works of charity.

Guarding chastity is necessary. But chastity leads to holiness only when at the same time it exalts charity to the utmost.

The vocation of the Daughter of Saint Anne is a vocation to spiritual motherhood. And a mother, when she is worthy of the name, is the least selfish of creatures, the least able to think of herself. Poverty: an essential element of the “sequela Christi.”

A) Poverty: key to the “kingdom”

1. From the perspective of religious life, poverty emerges as the radical element of the “sequela Christi.”

Detachment from earthly goods236, proclaimed by Christ as an indispensable condition for all who aspire to “possess the Kingdom,” becomes for the religious the fundamental commitment; and “go, sell what you own, and give the money to the poor; then come, follow me” (2) acquires the categorical and decisive force of an absolute command for whoever wishes to embrace “the virginal and poor way of life that Christ the Lord chose for himself and that the Virgin his Mother embraced” (3).

And being found in human form, he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross”237.

It is not a matter of simple deprivation of material goods but of the most radical and inconceivable of humiliations: God becoming man. “Emptied” to this extent, he appears on earth in the garb that could be, for the carnal eyes of humanity, the clearest “sign” of his mysterious existential self-impoverishment, of which he himself would in due time reveal:

3. This profound mystery of faith could be revealed only by Christ; and only after his resurrection could the disciples truly understand it and bear witness to it themselves. But already in the Old Testament there were those who, sensing the religious dimension of poverty, had translated it into a feeling of deep humility and expressed it in an attitude of serene acceptance of their own wretchedness and trusting expectation of God's help.

Animated by humble faith and by a hope that remained unshaken through centuries of deportation and slaughter240, the little “remnant of Israel” was able to preserve and hand on, down to Joachim and Anne, Zechariah and Elizabeth, the certainty that poverty of heart is the only true claim to the Father's love and mercy.

The Virgin's Magnificat and the preaching of John the Baptist would be the immediate foretelling of the “good news” Jesus would proclaim to the poor241, revealing, together with the mystery of the cross and the beatitudes, the Father's “overflowing riches of charity”242.

Whoever wishes “to follow Christ as proposed by the Gospel”243 must therefore first of all acquire a sincere awareness of his or her radical poverty.

Jesus Christ, “though he was rich, became poor, so that by his poverty we might become rich”244. Human beings, however, have no need to make themselves poor; they must simply recognize that they are poor and, especially if called to profess poverty in religious life, must feel immensely grateful, because God thereby offers them the most immediate and sure means of sharing in the riches of Christ's poverty; and therefore they must nourish in themselves his “mind” and strive to live inwardly this mystery of poverty, of which detachment from material goods is only the outward garment; and finally, always imitating Christ, they must practice the most perfect form of poverty of spirit, which consists in faithful and loving adherence to God's will in every circumstance of life.

4. To adhere to God in a spirit of poverty means joyfully accepting a condition of permanent precariousness in which, having nothing of one's own, one expects everything from God; having entrusted one's will to him in order to cooperate with Christ in carrying out the plan of salvation, one cannot dispose of one's own time or life but must be ready to respond to the signs of the divine will however made known; and, established in this loving and total availability to God in the service of others, one has renounced every stable tie of affection and condition of life.

This outlines the fundamental role of the virtue of poverty in relation to the other two constitutive elements of religious life, and the derivation of religious life itself from the three theological virtues, from which poverty, obedience and chastity draw their strength.

5. By the very fact of being a “Daughter of Saint Anne,” that is, a spiritual heir of the “poor of Yahweh,” the Daughter of Saint Anne is called to live in a quite particular way the poverty of Christ, who, “though master of all things, chose not to have a stone on which to lay his head”245, and therefore to accept with joy the state of earthly precariousness and supernatural security of one who has entrusted her life entirely to God, “supremely beloved”246.

The ideal of the most absolute poverty dominates Mother Rosa's very first inspiration: “Utterly poor!”247 is the cry that bursts from her heart in the face of proposals for mitigation; and in the Regulation of 1866 this will finds more formal but no less determined expression: “Nothing is to be accumulated, since any surplus must be distributed to the poor and to needy Churches”...248.

And just as Jesus' attention and preaching were directed mainly to the poor, so the care of the Daughters of Saint Anne, in carrying out their charitable work, was given preferably to the most wretched.

Their first charges were in fact the sick, and among them the favorites were those “abandoned by all” or who had “very repulsive illnesses,” because in them the first Daughters of Saint Anne saw “the passion of Jesus Christ more clearly expressed”249; and the “poor girls at risk,” that is, the young women most in need of material and moral assistance because of their particular state of neglect.

Through the vow of poverty, therefore, the Daughter of Saint Anne commits herself:

- to recognize and accept her radical poverty as a human creature, in a spirit of humility and simplicity, prudence and meekness;

- to live consistently with this real situation of hers, that is, in the material and spiritual condition of the truly poor, but with soul and face transfigured by the joy of the Beatitudes.

To the Daughter of Saint Anne, poor among the poor, God and the Church entrust a mission of witness and gift.

B) Concrete requirements of individual and community poverty

10. Religious poverty is first of all a theological and mystical requirement: Christ chose to be poor in order to reveal, under this visible garb, the profound renunciation constituted by the mystery of the Incarnation.

Religious cannot receive the life of Christ or accomplish in themselves the mystery of the redeeming Incarnation262 unless they follow and imitate him in his state of voluntary and affective poverty.

11. It is an ascetical requirement: voluntary renunciation of goods is an act of humility by which one recognizes and accepts one's natural condition of need and wretchedness, and an act of faith and hope by which one entrusts one's life to God, continually enlivened by prayer.

12. It is a psychological requirement: material poverty is the indispensable safeguard of poverty of spirit. It is not easy, indeed the Gospel says it is almost impossible263, for anyone to keep feelings, desires and attitudes detached from material riches when constantly exposed to their insidious allure.

13. It is a requirement of social justice: it is unjust and scandalous to present oneself to the world labeled as a professional of evangelical poverty while living in a condition of comfort and security most of humanity has never known.

14. Finally, it is an apostolic necessity: the truly poor will never be able to believe, much less accept, the Gospel message if it is proclaimed by people who are not what they claim to be.

Whoever wishes to be a brother or sister to the poor, as Christ was, will never understand their condition while actually standing outside it.

And although it is true that the mission of witness consists in proclaiming salvation to the poor rather than promising them wealth, it is also true that religious are called to a mission of active and effective charity that must help show the poor the ways and means of their human and Christian advancement264.

The Gospel message will be all the more acceptable, and concrete assistance all the more effective, the better the apostle knows how to stand on a level of encounter and exchange with the poor.

26. Poverty of spirit begets freedom of spirit. Therefore the practice of poverty, rightly understood, can never be a cause of anxiety and distress.

Excessive worry about what may wear out, be lost or be destroyed in carrying out works of charity and apostolate would rather betray attachment to goods, an instinct of avarice, and would be wholly opposed to that serene and joyful detachment from every material thing that marks the poor in spirit.

27. Since the sole end of religious life is the faithful fulfillment of God's will in activity placed at the service of others in imitation of Jesus Christ, it is logical and right to use with integrity, intelligence and good sense the means he provides for carrying out this service as well as possible.

28. It is good sense, then, that must establish a proper hierarchy of values both in the use and in the care of common goods.

The most precious good God entrusts to a Congregation is the person of its religious: their call to holiness, their intelligence, their aptitudes, their health, their life.

Besides being unjust, it would be foolish to care more for the upkeep of buildings or the efficiency of work tools, and worse still for money for its own sake, than for the spiritual and intellectual progress of the religious, the development and refinement of their aptitudes, and their health.

On the other hand, it would be a misguided liberality, fostering individual or community ambitions and feeding caste pride rather than promoting spiritual and apostolic growth, to have religious systematically obtain academic qualifications beyond what their office and the Institute's apostolic commitments require283, or to provide works with means disproportionately greater than the ends to be achieved.

In outward events, necessary as they may be, every trace of pomp, publicity display and triumphalism is moreover to be avoided; the witness the Church asks of religious does not consist in letting the world know what they do, but in living in the midst of the world as God and the Church want them to live.

29. As for care of health, the attitude of the religious concerned must be one thing, that of the Community toward him another. The sick religious must keep in mind his condition as one voluntarily poor, associated with Christ's passion and made certain by faith of the salvation Christ promised his faithful by virtue of his glorious resurrection. He will therefore accept with a humble and grateful heart the care given him, but will not claim as his right special and costly treatment beyond the reach of the truly poor.

The community, for its part, will lavish on the sick person, and on all religious without distinction when they are ill, all necessary care, both out of the charity it owes the brother or sister and out of the respect it owes to God, who has entrusted to it, in that person, a precious good to safeguard.

Before the Second Vatican Council, the spiritual role of the superior was conceived rather as that of a guardian of the Rule, whose observance constituted the perfection of religious life and came almost to be identified with the very end of religious life. Authority thus came down from above, and on the subjects lay the duty of a submission of will that was, if not exactly “blind,” at least passive, and of a common life founded on complete conformity.

The Second Vatican Council gave the religious superior the face of an animator from within, in a sense more horizontal than vertical. The Superior is a leader, yes, but above all because he is the one who, like Christ, gives himself to his brothers with complete dedication, so that they too may learn to give themselves with the same generosity to God and to others346. Indeed the Superior must also be the dynamic principle of the community's Gospel life, giving it the impetus of apostolic dedication in the spirit of the Constitutions, which in turn express the will God made known to the Founder347.

Dialogue and co-responsibility

His attitude must therefore be marked by warm openness, by a readiness for dialogue that allows exchange of views, comparison of standpoints and analysis of different experiences; all on the basis of calm discussion, from which it will be easier to draw new ideas and better solutions, and then to make decisions to which all will more readily adhere with heartfelt conviction.

41. Under the first conception of the exercise of superiorship it was perhaps easier to direct a community; but some restriction of the growth of community spirit and of personal initiative was inevitable, all ultimately to the detriment of apostolic activity and solely to the advantage of the material observance of the Rule and of uniformity in common life.

Under the second conception the spirit has much greater room to range; but the danger of harmful excesses is not excluded and must be avoided with tact, charity, personal dedication and a great deal of humility. The superior must therefore place himself, like Jesus among the disciples, on the same level and at times348 “as one who serves”; this is the only authentic way to exercise authority “in a spirit of service” and to express to his brothers “the charity with which God loves them”349 and the respect due “to children of God and human persons.” In this way he will succeed in having his word accepted with respect and love; a word that must be accepted, for it must not be forgotten that only the superior's approval can make valid a proposal of the community, even a collegial one.

42. Openness to dialogue fosters both the members' spiritual progress in charity and their apostolic activity; and this is of fundamental importance, especially since Vatican II affirmed that “apostolic and charitable activity belongs to the very nature of religious life” and that “intimate union with Christ” is the condition for responding to the vocation that calls them to follow Christ and serve him in his members. Called thus, as co-responsible, to direct participation in Christ's saving work in the Church, all religious must have an attitude of attentive listening to every message that comes from God through the voice of the Church, the signs of the times and the appeals of humanity350.

43. But for a religious the response to the message cannot be the fruit of a merely personal impulse. Co-responsibility does not cancel but rather increases the need for the superior's presence and authority.

The Holy Spirit may call anyone to a new initiative of charity, to a new apostolic activity. But by virtue of the vow of obedience, the religious can discern only with the superior's help what, in the light of the Institute's specific end, the concrete possibilities of the moment and the real abilities of the religious himself, God asks and expects, hic et nunc, of the individual and of the community351.

To walk the way of evangelical perfection according to the call received, the religious has chosen the means of obedience to a superior, a choice that involves his fruitful share in the divine plan of salvation. To the Superior belongs the task of mediator between God's will, the individual and the community.

44. On the other hand, the fact that each religious may put forward new ideas, propose initiatives and even carry the discussion to the practical level of a work in no way diminishes the spirit of dependence on the superior or on the Rule, provided that each adopts the fundamental disposition of seeking together, with docility of spirit, what God's will actually is regarding a given plan or the practical detail of a plan352.

in a climate of trust

After dialogue, the subsequent act of obedience can only be more committed and meritorious, because always and in every case the final decision, whether reached by consensus or responsibly dictated by the superior alone, must be regarded in the light of faith as the expression of God's authentic will.

Christ too, at the supreme moment, prayed: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; and only then added: “yet not what I want but what you want”353. What matters is that the same commitment to seeking God's authentic will should animate both subject and superior, beyond and above any reservation dictated by pride or personal interest.

45. The principle of the religious' co-responsibility and the very complexity of the tasks arising from it require the superior wisely to apply the principle of subsidiarity, assigning to each member of the community the tasks best suited to him, both on the practical and on the apostolic level354.

It is certain that harmony will reign in each community to the extent that each superior is able to give every religious the right place, enabling him to express his creativity and take on the degree of responsibility he is actually capable of; then and only then will each religious, recognized as an active and useful member, be esteemed and feel integrated and at peace.

46. But wisdom is not enough for the superior; he must also know how to inspire and show trust. Trust [in] his brothers, even at the calculated risk of a mistake, a straying or even a defection.

Religious men, and perhaps women religious even more, need to feel free from the fear of making mistakes in order to work well, especially when they know they cannot count on the affectionate understanding of the superior and consequently of their brothers or sisters; in such cases the fear of making mistakes leads them to bury their talents in the ground rather than face the risk of trading with them355.

Since all maturing proceeds by degrees, yet no degree of maturity guarantees absolutely against possible mistakes, the superior must constantly show the fatherly face of authority, especially toward those brothers who most need it or when they most need it: that is, when they feel less strong and less capable, when they have made a mistake or fear making one.

47. The same trust must be shown to the community as a whole: the Superior will keep it informed of situations affecting the common interest, seek its participation when important decisions must be made, “willingly listen” to proposals and suggestions and, whenever possible and appropriate, gladly put them into effect356.

Naturally, trust must not be separated from prudence, which will lead him to keep silent about matters that by their nature or for reasons of charity must remain confidential. But trust in general will be all the more possible and less dangerous the better the superior has succeeded in integrating each member into the community and fostering that family spirit which makes it “all for one and one for all,” to the great benefit of mutual charity and an equal growth of the works; without, however, neglecting to educate everyone in discretion, which is the foundation of every balanced social relationship.

48. But so much availability and spirit of service on the Superior's part would bear no fruit if the Community did not respond adequately. Setting aside certain more or less personal and servile marks of deference which in another historical and social context were not only understandable but might even seem obligatory, P.C. defines briefly the nature of the “humble submission” that must nonetheless be given to the superior.

It consists in placing “at the disposal both the powers of mind and will and the gifts of nature and grace in carrying out commands and fulfilling the offices assigned to them, realizing that they are giving their cooperation in building up the Body of Christ according to God's plan”357.

49. In other words, submission passes through the person of the superior in his role as mediator, but is directed to God, in an attitude of:

- absolute respect, which does not exclude candor and confidence;

- total availability, which presupposes detachment from self;

- diligent performance of assigned tasks, which requires good use of the gifts of nature and grace received from God and placed at his disposal;

- a spirit of faith, which gives the exact sense both of the nature of one's task (“cooperation in building up the Body of Christ”358) and of the person of the Superior, “God's representative”359.

50. All this becomes possible, and even relatively easy, only when the heart is truly emptied of self. Otherwise even the following statement sounds not only impossible but contradictory and absurd: “...religious obedience, far from lessening the dignity of the human person, leads it to full maturity by extending the freedom of the children of God”360.

It is, in reality, a difficult synthesis of opposites, because man lives in a state of continual tension between two opposite and irreconcilable poles: God and all that is not God. To overcome this tension, religious life offers its members “the help” of a more stable way of life, of excellent teaching for attaining perfection, of fraternal communion in the service of Christ, of a freedom strengthened by obedience... and the strength “to advance joyfully on the road of charity,” and thus to overcome more easily the worst danger that can threaten a human being: that of becoming a slave to oneself361362.

51. But this danger never entirely disappears. Only the virtue of obedience can prevent freedom from degenerating into license; and dignity will be truly safeguarded only by those who, in the school of Christ, have learned its only means: the folly of the cross363.

The new vision of religious life and of the virtue of obedience, tempered by the affirmation of the respect due to the human person364, therefore certainly does not authorize union-style attitudes of making demands or impatience toward authority. The model is always and only Christ, who came “not to be served but to serve” and became obedient to the point of death on a cross.

52. The theological motivation for obedience drawn from the Rule of 1869 expresses the same adherence to the Gospel that characterizes the Documents of Vatican II: “...my Institute, to honor the obedience of Jesus, who obeyed even the wicked and went so far as to die in obedience to his Divine Father... takes a vow of this virtue”365.

On the ascetical level, the norms laid down in the same Chapter VII of the Rules cannot, naturally, free themselves from the orientation, common at the time, toward predominantly external prescriptions, but they have the notable feature of prefacing the individual norms with their reasons, both spiritual and practical366. And in general the spiritual reasons almost instinctively bring out the close relationship between poverty of spirit and the practice of obedience.

53. Strikingly relevant today is the concept of the relationship that should exist between Superior and Sister; it clearly shows the source of the superior's authority: “... you will have an enlightened faith that makes you see in her (the Superior) the representative of Jesus Christ367, source of all authority... The Superior has her authority over you not by virtue of her natural gifts... nor even by virtue of her moral qualities... no, she holds her superiority because she was legitimately elected to that office by one who had the authority to do so.

Therefore, to find your superior, you will take your eyes off the creature and fix them on Jesus Christ, from whom the creature receives her superiority... know and hold for certain that the faults and sins with which your Superior may be filled do not lessen her authority over you in the least...”368.

54. In determining the hierarchy of powers, the ecclesial spirit that, within the limits allowed by the mentality of the time, characterized the origins of the Institute of the Daughters of Saint Anne is evident: “In my Institute there is a supreme representative, and she is the Superior General of the whole Institute; and it is to this Superior General that you vow obedience... you will obey her in all the things she commands you, provided they are not sinful and, moreover, are in conformity with the Rules of the Institute...” The Superior General has her lieutenants, who are the superiors she appoints to preside over the individual houses of the Institute. To them she confers part of the full authority she has over all:

“...you will obey this superior of the house where you are... with the same obedience with which you are bound to obey the General... hear, then, the order of Authority in my Institute: the superiors receive their authority from the Superior General, the Superior General receives it from the Pope, the Pope receives it from Jesus Christ; and so... by obeying your Superior you obey the Pope, you obey Jesus Christ. This clear distinction between the person of the superior and the dignity of her office establishes the exact norm for a balanced exercise of both authority and obedience.

D) Obedience and authority in the thought and life of Mother Rosa Gattorno

61. In Mother Rosa's way of conceiving obedience and authority, one can see that the Holy Spirit was her teacher: apart from a few marginal details, her conception fits perfectly within the spirit of Vatican II. Deeply aware of the supernatural value of obedience, and matured as she was in the school of Jesus Crucified, she understood perfectly that the exercise of authority in religious life is only a concrete way, sometimes the most difficult and painful, of practicing obedience: to God and to the Church.

Her obedience

62. She is a model of obedience as a daughter of her family and as a Christian wife. As a widow, she binds herself by a vow of obedience to her Confessor and depends on the diocesan Authority in all her works of charitable assistance. Called by God to a wider and tremendously demanding work, Rosa finds herself torn between two conflicting and equally imperative demands of obedience. She turns to the highest Authority, and to the Pope, who commands, she answers with a broken heart: “I want to do God's will.” In her very way of governing, while many virtues shine, two stand out above all: her loving attention to every sign of God's will, even when it costs her great sacrifices and sorrows; and her submission to the Church.

64. It is in love and for love that she exercises her office as foundress and superior general; a deep sense of responsibility stands out in her, expressed in a humble and generous spirit of service. She clearly realizes that her authority, like all authority, must simply be a mediation, the more perfect the more it succeeds in becoming a clear transparency of God. And she exercises a role of service for her daughters' souls, concerned solely with enlightening and guiding them by example. She feels responsible for every failing of others, so that she never reproves or corrects without taking on herself the greater part of the blame, as though she had not been able to foresee, prevent and avoid it sufficiently.

She tries to instill the same sense of responsibility in the Superiors: “Everything lies in knowing how to cultivate them (the sisters)... they are plants that dry up without fertilizer... a superior must try to do everything so that her sisters can drink their fill of the water our Master Jesus spoke of to the Samaritan woman... she must gather them often and give them fine exhortations... the Superior must, as far as she can, be among them...”380.

66. But she also grasped the meaning of “active and responsible obedience” and tries to instill it with complete freedom of spirit and complete trust in the radiant power of love: “Love and do what you will”381. It is one of her favorite expressions. She widely practices the principle of subsidiarity toward local superiors. Phrases like “Go ahead, you will do everything well,” or “tell me what you think,” “we will think about it together” are very frequent in her letters.

67. Every letter is proof of her trust in her daughters, whom she encourages with a warmth that shapes personality and develops a sense of responsibility and initiative.

Despite the disappointments she suffered, through her trust she ceaselessly shows the inexhaustible depth of her love and of the no less living faith from which she drew her unshakable optimism and which also nourished the sense of motherhood that in her was a gift of nature and of grace383.

68. Love took over her whole life. In charity and dedication she knows no limits. Every need she learns of is for her a call from God. So living and deep a love leaves her little time and arouses in her little interest in organizational and planning structures.

Nevertheless, she has no peace until she obtains approval of the Constitutions, because her deeply ecclesial spirit makes her understand that the Church's approval is a seal of authenticity and stability for God's Work. But her original and essential program is one alone: “the principal purpose of this Institute is to practice charity”384. And for her, that could suffice until the end of the world.

The discipline of religious life, the supreme responsibility of those in government, is a constant object of her concern385 and leads her to accept with humility and submission the restrictions canonical norms impose on her own activity and her daughters'. But she truly feels them as external impositions from which she gladly escapes, not through material transgressions, which the delicacy of her conscience as a devoted daughter of the Church would not allow, but with a beat of the wings that carries her beyond the written law into the regions of freedom of spirit. Hence the phrase “love and do what you will” expresses her whole asceticism. 70. If the life of the Daughter of Saint Anne, by God's providential will, is wholly permeated by the motherly presence of her holy Patroness, her nuptial union with Christ is illuminated by the presence of Mary, Daughter of Saint Anne and Mother of Jesus.

Prototype of virginal vocation at a time when this special relationship with the Lord was almost unknown, Mary “stands out among the poor and humble of the Lord, who confidently hope for and receive salvation from him”386.

In the poverty of her heart she accepts the Angel's announcement in perfect submission, placing her life within a mystery of faith that will become fully clear only on the day of the resurrection.

Beside her Son, yet lost in the crowd in humble silence, Mary “was a model of that motherly love by which all should be animated who cooperate in the apostolic mission of the Church for the regeneration of humanity”387.

All the distinctive aspects of Mary's life are found in the vocation of her younger sisters; not by chance, then, does the Rule of 1869 say: “If you want my spirit, you have only to paint in your mind the most beautiful... the most exact picture of my blessed Daughter.”

The Daughter of Saint Anne must therefore draw inspiration from Mary in diligently seeking God's will, in striving to cling ever more to Christ in total self-emptying, in fidelity to the Church, in which Christ's work continues and moves toward fulfillment, and in love for the souls Mary redeemed with the blood of her Son.

In the practice of obedience especially, the whole commitment of the Daughter of Saint Anne can be summed up in two phrases from the Virgin's lips:

- when she must obey: “Here am I, the servant of the Lord”;

At the Last Supper, the first Eucharist, he perpetuates in advance the memorial of his passion423, through which, “although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered; and having been made perfect, he became the source of eternal salvation for all”424. By his resurrection and ascension into heaven he completes the work the Father entrusted to him in his mortal life, leaving the community of believers “full of joy, praising and blessing God”425.

B) Like Mary, the servant of the Lord...

14. The Gospel, presenting the Virgin Mother of Jesus beside her Son who redeems the world426, allows us to glimpse in Mary's various attitudes the deepest feelings of humble openness to the Father and loving communion with others, in faithful docility to the Spirit.

15. A true Israelite, Mary is the revelation of the “little Remnant of Israel,” able to receive the promise and to cooperate closely in its fulfillment through the total availability of her “poor” heart. Her path was doubtless almost always one of silent listening in faith427, and so her prayer is the expression of her vocation as “servant of the Lord,” a title Mary explicitly gives herself at the moment of the Incarnation428 and reaffirms in the hymn of praise and gratitude of the Magnificat429, identifying herself with Israel, the chosen people Scripture calls “servant of the Lord.”

16. Yet in the various events of Jesus' hidden life, not always understandable, Mary “treasures all these things, pondering them in her heart”430; wholly consecrated “as handmaid of the Lord to the person and work of her Son, she serves the mystery of redemption under him and with him”431; at Cana her prayer of intercession brings about the first miracle432; present at Jesus' preaching, she merits the beatitude of those who hear and keep the Word of God433; on Calvary, beside the cross, she stands contemplating her Only-begotten, suffering deeply with him and associating herself with his sacrifice434. After Jesus' resurrection and ascension, she presides over the first Community of Disciples and implores “by her prayers the gift of the Spirit”435.

17. Supreme example of trust and abandonment to God, “the perfect example of spiritual and apostolic life is the Blessed Virgin Mary,” who, “while leading on earth a life common to all, filled with family concerns and labors, was always intimately united with her Son”436, summing up in the simplicity of her attitude as humble “servant of the Lord” the greatness of her communion with God and of her motherly love for humanity.

The poor keep the Law in their hearts,

consecrated to the Person and Work of the Son,

and express their praise of God

in the prayer of the Psalms,

and perfect model of spiritual and apostolic life.

C)... In the prayer of the poor...

18. The spirituality of the poor, formed through the events of the history of the people of Israel, founded its communion with God on the Covenant, a mystery of Yahweh's elective love437, who had revealed himself to his people: “...happy are we, O Israel, for we know what is pleasing to the Lord”438; and so every good Israelite keeps the Law in his heart: “Oh, how I love your law! It is my meditation all day long”439.

19. To seek Yahweh means not only to express in prayer and sacrifice the praise of adoration and thanksgiving440 but also to practice justice441, in an attitude of humble openness to his word, with full trust and firm hope, in the certainty that after suffering and humiliation the poor will be glorified and will share in the eternal joy promised to Abraham and his descendants442.

20. As Israel's praying voice, the Psalms express these feelings while showing the historical and personal situations from which they arise. They gather the echo of the cries that welled up from the people's heart through all the centuries; they reveal its inner religiousness, its zeal for justice and the defense of the weak, and give a prophetic vision of messianic times and events, foretelling the mysteries of the Savior's life443.

awaiting the Messiah.

docile to the action of the Spirit.

21. Animated by the hope of salvation, the Psalms are light and comfort through the long centuries preparing for Christ's coming and form the domestic and official prayer of Israel, within which stands Anne, the holy Mother of the Mother of God, who, in communion with her people, in humble, trusting and hidden prayer, awaits with tears and sighs the “desired of the Nations”444, the new shoot from the “root of Jesse”445.

Crucified

Identified with her “Crucified Beloved”

as a daughter before the Father,

D) In the footsteps of Mother Rosa...

22. Rosa Gattorno, on her way to God, did not take an abstract model as her inspiration but, moment by moment, in fidelity to the Spirit, lived out the imitation of Christ, the fundamental purpose of her existence, with ever-growing commitment. Letting herself be clothed with Christ446, she lived for him alone. “...I was not living; it was my Beloved who lived in me.” This expression, repeated continually in her “Memoirs,” confirms that her identification with the Lord consisted not so much in a moralistic interpretation of the Law as in allowing him to enter existentially into her personal history.

The Daughters of Saint Anne unite prayer and action

with the hearts of the poor,

and in Christ,

23. Discovering in God the sole Source of being, Rosa devoted herself with uncommon ardor to seeking his love alone447 and, clothed with the mind of Christ448, knew how to find her place “… shame and confusion I do not find.”

24. Docile to the action of her “Governing Spirit,” Rosa knows she is loved by God and loves him, and in wonderful familiarity with him she finds peace and joy in devoting herself to the poor, the abandoned and the suffering, because in them she recognizes her “Crucified Beloved.”
